Sequential Membership Inference Attacks

Thomas Michel Affiliation: Univ. Lille, Inria, CNRS, Centrale Lille, UMR 9189-CRIStAL, France Correspondence to: thomas.michel@inria.fr    Debabrota Basu Affiliation: Univ. Lille, Inria, CNRS, Centrale Lille, UMR 9189-CRIStAL, France    Emilie Kaufmann Affiliation: Univ. Lille, Inria, CNRS, Centrale Lille, UMR 9189-CRIStAL, France
Abstract

Modern AI models are not static. They go through multiple updates in their lifecycles. Thus, exploiting the model dynamics to create stronger Membership Inference (MI) attacks and tighter privacy audits are timely questions. Though the literature empirically shows that using a sequence of model updates can increase the power of MI attacks, rigorous analysis of the ‘optimal’ MI attacks is limited to static models with infinite samples. Hence, we develop an ‘optimal’ MI attack, SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*}, that uses the sequence of model updates to identify the presence of a target inserted at a certain update step. For the empirical mean computation, we derive the optimal power of SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*}, while accessing a finite number of samples with or without privacy. Our results retrieve the existing asymptotic analysis. We observe that having access to the model sequence avoids the dilution of MI signals unlike the existing attacks on the final model, where the MI signal vanishes as training data accumulates. Furthermore, an adversary can use SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*} to tune both the insertion time and the canary to yield tighter privacy audits. Finally, we conduct experiments across data distributions and models trained or fine-tuned with DP-SGD demonstrating that practical variants of SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*} lead to tighter privacy audits than the baselines.

Keywords: 
Membership Inference, Privacy Auditing, Differential Privacy, Model Updates, Hypothesis Testing

1 Introduction

Machine Learning (ML) models memorize training data, creating privacy risks for individuals whose data were used to develop them (Shokri et al., 2017; Carlini et al., 2022a). Privacy auditing quantifies these risks by testing whether specific records can be detected in the training set. Membership Inference (MI) attacks serve as the primary tool for auditing: an attacker who distinguishes members from non-members with high confidence establishes an empirical lower bound on the model’s privacy leakage (Jayaraman & Evans, 2019; Jagielski et al., 2020; Nasr et al., 2023). Audits with higher distinguishing power yield tighter bounds.

Privacy auditing has been developed to complement differential privacy (Dwork et al., 2006; Dwork & Roth, 2014). Early work establishes that even simple statistical models leak membership information (Homer et al., 2008). Theoretical analysis shows that privacy depends on the ratio of dimensionality to sample size (Sankararaman et al., 2009). Jayaraman & Evans (2019) found 5–10×\times gaps between theoretical DP guarantees and empirical privacy estimates. Techniques for tight auditing (Nasr et al., 2023; Steinke et al., 2023) and debugging (Tramer et al., 2022) close this gap by crafting adversarial targets and observing model updates during training. Our approach shows how exploiting intermediate observations can yield tighter privacy audits.

Specifically, standard auditing practice targets a specific snapshot of a model. The auditor selects a target point (a.k.a. canary), queries the model, and applies a membership test. Target selection matters: points ‘far’ from the data distribution leak more information than typical points (Azize & Basu, 2025; Carlini et al., 2022b). Modern ML models are dynamic: they rarely exist as isolated snapshots. Continuous training updates the deployed models as new data arrives. Fine-tuning adapts the base models to specific tasks. Federated learning aggregates updates from different users across rounds. In each case, multiple model versions become accessible, whether through public release, API versioning, or checkpoint access during training.

Jagielski et al. (2023) demonstrate that combining the MI scores across model updates improves attack accuracy. They apply standard MI attacks separately to each model snapshot, and then, aggregate the scores via difference or ratio operations. Related work on model updates includes reconstruction attacks (Salem et al., 2020) that recover data from online learning updates, machine unlearning attacks (Chen et al., 2020), and leakage analysis of snapshots in NLP (Zanella-Béguelin et al., 2020). Our approach differs by deriving the optimal test via likelihood ratio analysis and identifying the insertion time of a canary as a new actionable lever for tighter audits.

We study Membership Inference (MI) when the auditor observes a sequence of TT model snapshots rather than a single static one. The sequential setting offers two levers for designing tight audits: selecting targets that leak information, and choosing when to insert them. Specifically, we ask:

1. Are there advantages of the MI tests accessing a sequence of models in comparison to a static test on the final model?
2. Does the knowledge of the insertion time affect the power of sequential MI tests?
3. Can sequential MI tests lead to theoretically and practically tighter privacy audits?

Our contributions address these questions affirmatively.

(1) Optimal MI test with sequential access. Motivated by the optimal MI attack for the static setting (Azize & Basu, 2025) derived from the Neyman-Pearson lemma (Neyman & Pearson, 1933), we derive the optimal MI attack in the sequential setting, which is a sequential likelihood ratio test crafted with an insertion time. We refer to it as SeMI∗. Specifically, for the empirical mean computation from Gaussian data, we derive a closed-form analysis of the sequential MI attack.

(2) Isolation property of sequential MI test. We further observe a unique phenomenon for the sequential MI test on the empirical mean, namely isolation property. This means that consecutive outputs reveal the batch mean at insertion time τ\tau exactly. The likelihood ratio depends only on this recovered batch statistic. Rather than detecting the target among all cumulative samples, the sequential test operates on an isolated batch of size nn. For the empirical mean under stationary conditions, test power depends only on batch size and target distance from the mean, not on τ\tau or TT. By contrast, a single-observation test applied to the final output must detect the target among n​TnT samples; its influence diminishes as training data accumulates. Sequential observation eliminates this dilution.

(3) Adapting MI tests with the insertion time. As insertion time emerges as a unique lever for sequential MI tests, we study the impact of the knowledge of the insertion time. We study three likelihood ratio based tests, SeMI∗, SeMIunif and SeMImax, that respectively assume τ\tau is known, uniformly distributed, or can be anything. We derive their powers for the empirical mean mechanism. Our numerical studies show that SeMI∗ achieves the best power while the other two behave similarly.

(4) Extending sequential MI tests to Gradient Descent (GD). Since GD-type algorithms (Kiefer & Wolfowitz, 1952) and their variants are the standard to train modern ML models, we further extend the design of sequential MI tests to Stochastic GD (SGD) and DP-SGD (Abadi et al., 2016) for batch training, namely SeMISGD. We clarify the practical relaxations needed to extend the sequential MI tests to the practical ML models. Our numerical studies for SGD and DP-SGD show similar improvements achieved by the sequential MI test and impact of the insertion time as in the empirical mean setting.

(5) From tighter sequential MI tests to sequential privacy audits. First, we formalize sequential privacy auditing as a hypothesis testing game that encodes the auditor’s control over target selection and insertion time. We test the proposed sequential privacy audit with SeMI for private fine-tuning of models with DP-SGD. Experimental results across datasets, models, and pre-defined privacy levels illustrate that SeMISGD generally exhibits tighter privacy audits than the baselines, especially in the high privacy regimes.

2 Auditing and Membership Inference for Sequential Mechanisms

We assume data is sequentially collected over TT steps. At each step t∈{1,…,T}t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}, a fresh batch of data DtD_{t} consisting of nn samples arrives. Each sample is drawn i.i.d. from a distribution 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t}. At step tt, a sequential mechanism ℳt\mathcal{M}_{t} is applied to the accumulated dataset, releasing output ot≜ℳt​(⋃i=1tDi)o_{t}\triangleq\mathcal{M}_{t}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{t}D_{i}\right). We let ℳ\mathcal{M} denote the composed global mechanism whose input is the joint dataset D≜⋃i=1TDiD\triangleq\bigcup_{i=1}^{T}D_{i} and output is the whole sequence o≜(o1,…,oT)o\triangleq(o_{1},\dots,o_{T}) obtained via the intermediate mechanisms ℳ1,…,ℳT\mathcal{M}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{M}_{T}. This formalism models an ML system which is retrained as new data arrives, and each version is released or accessible to users. The mechanisms and distributions may vary over time. We are interested in assessing the privacy level achieved by the global mechanism ℳ\mathcal{M}, while having access to the intermediate mechanisms ℳ1,…,ℳT\mathcal{M}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{M}_{T}.

To quantify the privacy level of a mechanism, we adhere to the classical (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-Differential Privacy (DP) framework (Dwork & Roth, 2014). ℳ\mathcal{M} satisfies (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP if for all measurable sets of output SS and datasets D,D′D,D^{\prime} differing in one element, and some ε>0\varepsilon>0 and δ∈[0,1)\delta\in[0,1),

Pr[ℳ(D)∈S]⩽eεPr[ℳ(D′)∈S]+δ.\Pr[\mathcal{M}(D)\in S]\leqslant e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[\mathcal{M}(D^{\prime})\in S]+\delta\,. (1)

Given some δ\delta, privacy auditing amounts to finding a lower bound on ε\varepsilon for which the inequality (1) is satisfied.

There are two dominant approaches to auditing. The first is to estimate the maximum ε\varepsilon for which max{Pr[ℳ(D)∈S]−eεPr[ℳ(D′)∈S],0}\max\{\Pr[\mathcal{M}(D)\in S]-e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[\mathcal{M}(D^{\prime})\in S],0\}, known as the hockey-stick divergence, is less than δ\delta (Koskela & Mohammadi, 2024; Basu & Chanda, 2026). The second is to leverage the hypothesis testing interpretation of DP (Wasserman & Zhou, 2010; Kairouz et al., 2015) that conducts MI tests and uses the error probabilities of the tests to create a lower bound on ε\varepsilon. As the second approach additionally provides insights for designing optimal MI tests and the most privacy leaking canaries (Nasr et al., 2023; Azize & Basu, 2025), we explore it for the sequential mechanisms.

MI tests are binary hypothesis tests that try to identify whether a particular target z∗z^{*} is present in the input dataset DD by observing the output of a mechanism (Carlini et al., 2022a; Ye et al., 2022; Leemann et al., 2023). Furthermore, a crafter is deployed to design a canary z∗z^{*}, and then, to decide whether to insert z∗z^{*} in the dataset or not.

In the sequential model access setting, we further ask whether z∗z^{*} belongs to a specific sub-dataset DτD_{\tau}, where τ∈ℕ\tau\in\mathbb{N} denotes the insertion time. Specifically, as we observe the model updates one by one, a sequential MI test works with two hypothesis classes parameterized by z∗z^{*}:

𝐇𝟎​(OUT):\mathbf{H_{0}}~(\text{OUT}): D∼𝒫0D\sim\mathcal{P}_{0}, if for all t∈[T]t\in[T], Dt∼𝒟t⊗nD_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}^{\otimes n}.

𝐇𝟏​(IN):\mathbf{H_{1}}~(\text{IN}): D∼𝒫1τD\sim\mathcal{P}_{1}^{\tau}, if for all t∈[T]t\in[T], Dt∼𝒟t⊗nD_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}^{\otimes n}, and then given J∼𝒰⁡([n])J\sim\mathcal{U}([n]), the JJ-th entry of DτD_{\tau} is replaced by z∗z^{*}.

We define a probability model parameterized by νB\nu_{B}, i.e., a distribution over {0,1}\{0,1\}, and ντ\nu_{\tau}, i.e., a distribution over {1,…,T}\{1,\dots,T\}. Under this model, we draw an insertion indicator B∼νBB\sim\nu_{B} and an insertion time τ∼ντ\tau\sim\nu_{\tau}. If B=0B=0, we draw D∼𝒫0D\sim\mathcal{P}_{0}. If B=1B=1, we draw D∼𝒫1τD\sim\mathcal{P}^{\tau}_{1}. The mechanism ℳ\mathcal{M} produces output (o1,…,oT)(o_{1},\dots,o_{T}). A sequential MI test 𝒜\mathcal{A} maps the output sequence to a prediction B^=𝒜z∗,τ​(o1,…,oT)\widehat{B}=\mathcal{A}_{z^{*},\tau}(o_{1},\dots,o_{T}), where the subscript indicates that the test depends on the target z∗z^{*} and the insertion time τ\tau. Algorithm 2 formalizes the Sequential Membership Inference (SeMI) game used to estimate these error rates, whereas Algorithm 1 demonstrates a crafter that leverages a distribution ντ\nu_{\tau} over insertion time to choose the exact step τ\tau, where it inserts the canary in the dataset.

Lemma 2.1 (Connecting MI Test Error and Privacy Audits (Kairouz et al., 2015)).

Let α⁡(𝒜)≜ℙ⁡(B^=1|B=0)\alpha(\mathcal{A})\triangleq\mathbb{P}(\widehat{B}=1|B=0) and β⁡(𝒜)≜ℙ⁡(B^=0|B=1)\beta(\mathcal{A})\triangleq\mathbb{P}(\widehat{B}=0|B=1) be the Type I and Type II errors of an MI test 𝒜\mathcal{A}, respectively. If the mechanism ℳ\mathcal{M} is (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP, the following holds for any MI test

α⁡(𝒜)+eε​β​(𝒜)\displaystyle\alpha(\mathcal{A})+e^{\varepsilon}\beta(\mathcal{A}) ⩾1−δ,β⁡(𝒜)+eε​α​(𝒜)⩾1−δ.\displaystyle\geqslant 1-\delta,\quad\beta(\mathcal{A})+e^{\varepsilon}\alpha(\mathcal{A})\geqslant 1-\delta.

Consequently, any MI test 𝒜\mathcal{A} provides the following lower bound on ε\varepsilon:

ε⩾log⁡(max⁡[1−δ−α⁡(𝒜)β⁡(𝒜),1−δ−β⁡(𝒜)α⁡(𝒜)]).\varepsilon\geqslant\log\left(\max\left[\frac{1-\delta-\alpha(\mathcal{A})}{\beta(\mathcal{A})},\frac{1-\delta-\beta(\mathcal{A})}{\alpha(\mathcal{A})}\right]\right). (2)

A practical lower bound further requires upper bounds on α⁡(𝒜)\alpha(\mathcal{A}) and β⁡(𝒜)\beta(\mathcal{A}) that can be obtained from multiple executions of the MI test (i.e. from the output of Algorithm 2). In Section 5, we provide a concrete instantiation of these error upper bounds for MI tests that threshold some test statistic, as well as the resulting high-probability lower bound on ε\varepsilon.

To obtain a tight lower bound, we seek to design a crafter and a sequential MI test (often called an adversary in auditing literature) that together achieve least possible α\alpha and β\beta, i.e. maximum accuracy in SeMI game.

The connection to statistical hypothesis testing guides the design of effective adversaries. Here, we consider the white-box setting (Sablayrolles et al., 2019; Carlini et al., 2022a; Nasr et al., 2023; Maddock et al., 2023), where the adversary observes the sequence of data distributions (𝒟t)(\mathcal{D}_{t}) and mechanisms (ℳt)(\mathcal{M}_{t}), batch size nn, and total steps TT.

When τ\tau is also known, computing B^\widehat{B} is a test of

𝐇𝟎​(OUT):(D∼𝒫0)​ against ​𝐇τ​(INτ):(D∼𝒫1τ)\displaystyle\mathbf{H_{0}}~(\text{OUT}):(D\sim\mathcal{P}_{0})\text{ against }\mathbf{H_{\tau}}~(\text{IN}_{\tau}):(D\sim\mathcal{P}_{1}^{\tau}) (3)

based on observing (o1,…,oT)(o_{1},\dots,o_{T}). When τ\tau is unknown to the adversary, so that B^=𝒜z∗​(o1,…,oT)\widehat{B}=\mathcal{A}_{z^{*}}(o_{1},\dots,o_{T}), the test becomes

𝐇𝟎~​(OUT):(D∼𝒫0)​ against ​𝐇𝟏~​(IN):(D∼𝒫~1),\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbf{H_{0}}}~(\text{OUT}):(D\sim\mathcal{P}_{0})\ \text{ against }\ \widetilde{\mathbf{H_{1}}}~(\text{IN}):(D\sim\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_{1}), (4)

where 𝒫~1\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_{1} is defined as τ∼ντ\tau\sim\nu_{\tau} and then D|τ∼𝒫1τD|\tau\sim\mathcal{P}_{1}^{\tau}.

When the data-generating distributions 𝒟1,…,𝒟T\mathcal{D}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{D}_{T} are known, both the problems reduce to testing simple hypotheses, for which the Neyman-Pearson lemma (Neyman & Pearson, 1933) establishes Likelihood Ratio (LR) tests to be optimal. Since the SeMI provides sequential access of the mechanisms, the question is: How to use the sequence of input-output data to compute a sequence of LR statistics and combine them over time to design efficient SeMI tests?

In the next sections, we design multiple SeMI tests that lead to tighter bounds on ε\varepsilon than the optimal MI test having access to only the final model.

3 Sequential Membership Inference

For theoretical rigor, we commence with the empirical mean mechanism of Gaussian data and derive the closed-form expressions of three SeMI tests: one knowing the insertion time, one assuming it be uniformly random and one considering the worst case. We show that knowing τ\tau yields the most powerful SeMI test, SeMI∗, which is also significantly better than having access to only the final model.

3.1 Optimal Test: SeMI∗

We analyze the empirical mean mechanism ℳemp\mathcal{M}^{\text{emp}} in a stationary setting, where 𝒟t=𝒟=𝒩⁡(𝝁,𝚺)\mathcal{D}_{t}=\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) for all tt, with mean vector 𝝁∈ℝd\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and a positive definite covariance matrix 𝚺∈ℝd×d\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. Connection to the Asymptotic Results. The test statistic depends on the target through its Mahalanobis distance m∗m^{*}, i.e., targets farther from the population mean in the metric induced by 𝚺−1\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} are more detectable. This parallels the asymptotic analysis of Azize & Basu (2025) showing that MI power scales with the Mahalanobis distance when both dd and n→∞n\rightarrow\infty and dn=𝒪⁡(1)\frac{d}{n}=\mathcal{O}(1). Our result provides the exact finite-sample likelihood ratio that yields an additional quadratic term in 𝐍τ\mathbf{N_{\tau}}. This term becomes negligible as n→∞n\to\infty and we retrieve their test statistic.

Remark 3.3 (Isolation Property).

We observe that given consecutive observations (μ^τ−1,μ^τ)(\hat{\mu}_{\tau-1},\hat{\mu}_{\tau}), the batch mean can be exactly recovered, i.e., X¯τ=τ​μ^τ−(τ−1)​μ^τ−1\bar{X}_{\tau}=\tau\hat{\mu}_{\tau}-(\tau-1)\hat{\mu}_{\tau-1}. Thus, the likelihood ratio depends on the data only through X¯τ\bar{X}_{\tau}. Since it is independent of the batches before and after, and also TT, we refer to it as the isolation property of SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*}.

The linear term captures alignment between the batch mean and the target direction, while the negative quadratic term penalizes large deviations from the population mean. The constant terms depend only on the signal strength (z∗−μ)/σ(z^{*}-\mu)/\sigma and the batch size nn.

Lemma 3.5 (Type I Error).

α⁡(γ)=Φ⁡(a+b⁡(γ))−Φ⁡(a−b⁡(γ))\alpha(\gamma)=\Phi(a+b(\gamma))-\Phi(a-b(\gamma))

where m∗=(z∗−μ)2σ2m^{*}=\frac{(z^{*}-\mu)^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}, a=m∗​na=\sqrt{m^{*}n} and b⁡(γ)=(n−1)​(m∗−log⁡(1−1n)−2​γ)b(\gamma)=\sqrt{(n-1)\left(m^{*}-\log\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)-2\gamma\right)}.

For γ⩽γmax\gamma\leqslant\gamma_{\max}, with aa and b⁡(γ)b(\gamma) as defined above:

β⁡(γ)\displaystyle\beta(\gamma) =Φ⁡(a​n−1n−b⁡(γ)​nn−1)\displaystyle=\Phi\left(a\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{n}}-b(\gamma)\sqrt{\frac{n}{n-1}}\right)

This τ\tau-invariance follows from the isolation property, i.e., the test operates on the recovered batch mean X¯τ\bar{X}_{\tau}, which has the same distribution regardless of when the insertion occurred.

Comparison with the Final Observation Test. When only the final output μ^T\hat{\mu}_{T} is observed, the test statistic has the same form, but with nn replaced by n​TnT. We call this baseline the Final Observation test.

βFO​(γ)\displaystyle\beta_{\mathrm{FO}}(\gamma) =Φ⁡(aT​n​T−1n​T−bT​(γ)​n​Tn​T−1)\displaystyle=\Phi\left(a_{T}\sqrt{\frac{nT-1}{nT}}-b_{T}(\gamma)\sqrt{\frac{nT}{nT-1}}\right)

SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*} operates on a batch of size nn, while Final Observation test must detect the target among n​TnT samples. As TT increases, the target’s signal (z∗−μ)/(n​T)(z^{*}-\mu)/(nT) vanishes for Final Observation, while SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*} retains constant power.

Remark 3.9 (Adapting to Distribution Shifts).

The analysis of SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*} extends to the non-stationary setting, where Dt∼𝒩⁡(μt,σt2)D_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{t},\sigma_{t}^{2}). The likelihood ratio depends only on (μτ,στ2)(\mu_{\tau},\sigma_{\tau}^{2}), while for t≠τt\neq\tau, conditioning on μ^t−1\hat{\mu}_{t-1} yields identical distributions under both hypotheses. The extension with time-varying parameters is given in Appendix C.

3.2 Adapting SeMI with Insertion Times

We now ask: what is the best possible MI test that is agnostic to τ\tau? This models an adversary who knows that the target z⋆z_{\star} may have been inserted but does not know when.

As discussed in Section 2, such an MI test can be obtained from a statistical test in which the alternative is 𝐇𝟏~\widetilde{\mathbf{H_{1}}}: τ\tau is drawn from ντ\nu_{\tau} (the distribution used by Crafter) and then the dataset is generated from 𝒫1τ\mathcal{P}_{1}^{\tau}. Since both 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}} and 𝐇𝟏~\widetilde{\mathbf{H_{1}}} specify complete distributions over the observations, the Neyman-Pearson lemma also applies, i.e., the optimal test thresholds the likelihood ratio.

Optimal test for uniform τ\tau. For ντ≜𝒰⁡({1,…,T})\nu_{\tau}\triangleq\mathcal{U}(\{1,\dots,T\}), we give the expression of the likelihood ratio, LRUnif\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{Unif}}. We call SeMIUnif\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{Unif}} the test that thresholds log⁡LRUnif\log\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{Unif}}.

Theorem 3.10 (Uniform τ\tau Likelihood Ratio).

Let LRt\mathrm{LR}_{t} be the likelihood ratio for 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}} against 𝐇𝟏𝐭\mathbf{H_{1}^{t}} from Theorem 3.1. The likelihood ratio for testing 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}} against 𝐇𝟏~\widetilde{\mathbf{H_{1}}} is

LRUnif=1T​∑t=1TLRt.\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{Unif}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathrm{LR}_{t}\,.

The marginal likelihood under 𝐇𝟏~\widetilde{\mathbf{H_{1}}} is obtained by averaging over τ\tau, i.e., conditioned on τ=t\tau=t, the data distribution matches 𝐇𝟏𝐭\mathbf{H_{1}^{t}}, so the marginal is (1/T)​∑tP⁡(data∣𝐇𝟏𝐭)(1/T)\sum_{t}P(\text{data}\mid\mathbf{H_{1}^{t}}). Dividing by the null likelihood yields the arithmetic mean of individual likelihood ratios. Details in Appendix D.

Relation to a GLR test. Using that maxt⁡LRt⩽∑t=1TLRt⩽T​maxt​LRt\max_{t}\mathrm{LR}_{t}\leqslant\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathrm{LR}_{t}\leqslant T\max_{t}\mathrm{LR}_{t} yields

maxt⁡log⁡LRt−log⁡T⩽log⁡LRUnif⩽maxt⁡log⁡LRt.\max_{t}\log\mathrm{LR}_{t}-\log T\leqslant\log\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{Unif}}\leqslant\max_{t}\log\mathrm{LR}_{t}\;.

This shows that SeMIUnif\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{Unif}} is quite close to the test that uses maxt⁡log⁡LRt\max_{t}\log\mathrm{LR}_{t} as a test statistic. We call it SeMImax\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{max}}. Interestingly, SeMImax\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{max}} can be interpreted as a Generalized Likelihood Ratio test (Zeitouni et al., 2002; Van Trees, 2004) of 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}} against ⋃t𝐇𝟏𝐭\bigcup_{t}\mathbf{H_{1}^{t}}. This is a composite hypothesis testing problem and there are no optimality guarantees for the resulting GLR test, but its connexion to SeMIUnif\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{Unif}} suggests that it can also lead to a good MI test.

In Section 3.3, we observe from experimental results that SeMIUnif\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{Unif}} and SeMImax\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{max}} have comparable performance, and they are both outperformed by SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*}. We further conjecture that replacing the uniform distribution by another distribution would lead to comparable performance.

3.3 Numerical Analysis: Sequential Advantage

The theoretical analysis identifies three aspects of the sequential advantage, i.e. accessing the sequence of models rather than only the final one.

First, isolation: SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*} produces a discrete jump in the test statistic at τ\tau with stable separation thereafter.

Second, power: SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*} achieves higher power than Final Observation at all false positive rates, with the gap widening as the target’s Mahalanobis distance increases.

Third, scaling with TT: SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*} power remains constant as TT increases (since it depends only on batch size nn), while Final Observation power degrades (since the target’s influence diminishes among n​TnT samples).

We illustrate these properties using the Gaussian empirical mean mechanism. We sample T=10T=10 batches of size n=10n=10 from 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1). The target z∗=3z^{*}=3 (Mahalanobis distance 3 from the distribution) is inserted at τ=5\tau=5.

Figure 2 tracks the log-likelihood ratio for a target inserted at τ=5\tau=5. The SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*} statistic exhibits a sharp, sustained step at τ\tau, effectively isolating the signal. In contrast, the Final Observation statistic shows a smaller jump that diminishes as TT grows, illustrating how the signal dilutes over time.

Figure 2 compares SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*} (known τ\tau) against SeMIUnif\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{Unif}}, SeMImax\mathrm{SeMI}^{\max}, and Final Observation. As predicted, SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*} maintains constant power regardless of TT, confirming the isolation property. While SeMIUnif\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{Unif}} and SeMImax\mathrm{SeMI}^{\max} degrade with TT, they consistently outperform Final Observation, especially for targets far from the distribution mean (high Mahalanobis distance). The errors are estimated using R=50,000R=50,000 runs of SeMI with ντ=δ{τ}\nu_{\tau}=\delta_{\{\tau\}} in the Crafter. Similar results are obtained for ντ=𝒰⁡([T])\nu_{\tau}=\mathcal{U}([T]). ROC curves and results under uniformly sampled τ\tau appear in Appendix H.1, displaying very similar dynamics to the fixed τ\tau case. Appendix H.3 shows that test power depends on the Mahalanobis distance rather than the data dimension dd.

4 Sequential MI for Gradient Descent

The empirical mean analysis establishes the sequential advantage in an idealized setting. To audit real ML models, we need tests that apply to gradient descent, the algorithm used to train virtually all modern models. Prior sequential attacks on SGD rely on heuristic score combinations (Jagielski et al., 2023). A principled likelihood ratio test for SGD would enable tighter privacy audits by exploiting the same isolation property that benefits the empirical mean.

We observe model parameters θ0,θ1,…,θT\theta_{0},\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{T} with θt∈ℝd\theta_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. At each step tt, the update is θt=θt−1−ηt​gt\theta_{t}=\theta_{t-1}-\eta_{t}g_{t} where ηt>0\eta_{t}>0 is the learning rate and gt=1nt​∑x∈Dt∇θℓ​(θt−1,x)g_{t}=\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{x\in D_{t}}\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{t-1};x) is the batch gradient on dataset DtD_{t} of size ntn_{t}. As in Section 3, we test 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}} (target z∗z^{*} not in the training data) against 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}} (target inserted in batch DτD_{\tau}).

4.1 Sequential Test for SGD

We assume that, conditioned on θt−1\theta_{t-1}, the batch gradient gtg_{t} is Gaussian with mean μg​(θt−1)\mu_{g}(\theta_{t-1}) and covariance Σg​(θt−1)/nt\Sigma_{g}(\theta_{t-1})/n_{t}. This approximation can be justified by the central limit theorem when the batch aggregates gradients from many data points.

Under this assumption, the conditional distributions mirror the empirical mean case. Under 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}: for all tt,

θt|θt−1,𝐇𝟎∼𝒩⁡(θt−1−ηt​μg​(θt−1),ηt2​Σg​(θt−1)nt).\theta_{t}\mid\theta_{t-1},\mathbf{H_{0}}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\theta_{t-1}-\eta_{t}\mu_{g}(\theta_{t-1}),\frac{\eta_{t}^{2}\Sigma_{g}(\theta_{t-1})}{n_{t}}\right).

Under 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}}with one sample in DτD_{\tau} replaced by target z∗z^{*}:

θτ|θτ−1,𝐇𝟏τ∼𝒩⁡(CLOSE\displaystyle\theta_{\tau}\mid\theta_{\tau-1},\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigg( θτ−1−ητ​(nτ−1)​μg+g∗nτ,\displaystyle\theta_{\tau-1}-\eta_{\tau}\frac{(n_{\tau}-1)\mu_{g}+g^{*}}{n_{\tau}},
OPENητ2​(nτ−1)​Σgnτ2)\displaystyle\frac{\eta_{\tau}^{2}(n_{\tau}-1)\Sigma_{g}}{n_{\tau}^{2}}\bigg)

where g∗=∇θℓ​(θτ−1,z∗)g^{*}=\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{\tau-1};z^{*}) is the target gradient, and we write μg\mu_{g} and Σg\Sigma_{g} for μg​(θτ−1)\mu_{g}(\theta_{\tau-1}) and Σg​(θτ−1)\Sigma_{g}(\theta_{\tau-1}).

The likelihood ratio factorizes as in Lemma 3.2: only the transition at time τ\tau contributes.

Theorem 4.1 (SeMISGD Log Likelihood Ratio).

Define δg=∇θℓ​(θτ−1,z∗)−μg​(θτ−1)\delta_{g}=\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{\tau-1};z^{*})-\mu_{g}(\theta_{\tau-1}) and N=θτ−θτ−1+ητ​μg​(θτ−1)N=\theta_{\tau}-\theta_{\tau-1}+\eta_{\tau}\mu_{g}(\theta_{\tau-1}). The log likelihood ratio is:

log⁡LR\displaystyle\log\mathrm{LR} =−d2​log⁡(nτ−1nτ)−nτ2​(nτ−1)​ητ2​N⊤​Σg−1​N\displaystyle=-\frac{d}{2}\log\left(\frac{n_{\tau}-1}{n_{\tau}}\right)-\frac{n_{\tau}}{2(n_{\tau}-1)\eta_{\tau}^{2}}N^{\top}\Sigma_{g}^{-1}N
−nτ(nτ−1)​ητ​N⊤​Σg−1​δg−m∗2​(nτ−1)\displaystyle\quad-\frac{n_{\tau}}{(n_{\tau}-1)\eta_{\tau}}N^{\top}\Sigma_{g}^{-1}\delta_{g}-\frac{m^{*}}{2(n_{\tau}-1)}

where m∗=δg⊤​Σg−1​δgm^{*}=\delta_{g}^{\top}\Sigma_{g}^{-1}\delta_{g} is the Mahalanobis distance of the target gradient from the population mean.

The test statistic SeMISGD\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{SGD}} has the same structure as Theorem 3.1, with the batch mean replaced by the scaled parameter update N/ητN/\eta_{\tau}. δg\delta_{g} measures how much the target’s gradient deviates from the population mean of the gradient: targets whose gradients differ substantially from typical gradients are more detectable. The Mahalanobis distance m∗m^{*} accounts for the gradient covariance structure, giving less weight to directions with high variance.

Isolation Property for SGD.

From consecutive parameter observations (θτ−1,θτ)(\theta_{\tau-1},\theta_{\tau}), the scaled update NN can be computed exactly. The likelihood ratio depends only on this quantity, not on earlier or later parameters. This mirrors the isolation property for the empirical mean.

Numerical Analysis: Linear Regression.

Unlike the empirical mean setting, where the population statistics are fixed, SGD introduces a complication: the gradient mean μg​(θ)\mu_{g}(\theta) and covariance Σg​(θ)\Sigma_{g}(\theta) vary with the model parameters. This variation means that a target may be easier to detect at certain stages of training than others, depending on how the test statistic evolves along the optimization trajectory. Experiments on linear regression with Gaussian data confirm that SeMISGD\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{SGD}} achieves higher power than heuristic baselines, and that insertion time affects power, although differently depending on the method (Appendix H.2). Section 5 extends this comparison to privacy auditing on real datasets.

4.2 Practical Extensions

In order to practically use SeMISGD\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{SGD}} for privacy audits of neural networks, we need to first adapt it to the private variant of SGD, called DP-SGD (Abadi et al., 2016), and estimate three quantities: the population mean gradient μg​(θτ−1)\mu_{g}(\theta_{\tau-1}), the gradient covariance Σg​(θτ−1)\Sigma_{g}(\theta_{\tau-1}), and the target gradient ∇θℓ​(θτ−1,z∗)\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{\tau-1};z^{*}).

Application to DP-SGD.

For differentially private training via DP-SGD, each update includes clipped gradients and Gaussian noise: θt=θt−1−ηt​(gtclip+ξt)\theta_{t}=\theta_{t-1}-\eta_{t}(g_{t}^{\mathrm{clip}}+\xi_{t}) where ξt∼𝒩⁡(0,σDP2​C2​I/nt2)\xi_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\mathrm{DP}}^{2}C^{2}I/n_{t}^{2}) with clipping threshold CC. The noise reduces test power but preserves the sequential structure and the isolation property. Section 5 applies SeMISGD\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{SGD}} to privacy auditing of DP-SGD fine-tuning on real datasets.

Estimation with Reference Data.

Since, in practice, the three quantities of interest in Theorem 4.1 are not known, the adversary estimates μg\mu_{g} and Σg\Sigma_{g} from reference data drawn from the same distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Given mm reference samples {x1,…,xm}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}\}, we compute μ^g=1m​∑i=1m∇θℓ​(θτ−1,xi)\hat{\mu}_{g}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{\tau-1};x_{i}), and Σ^g=1m−1​∑i=1m(∇θℓ​(θτ−1,xi)−μ^g)​(∇θℓ​(θτ−1,xi)−μ^g)⊤\hat{\Sigma}_{g}=\frac{1}{m-1}\sum_{i=1}^{m}(\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{\tau-1};x_{i})-\hat{\mu}_{g})(\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{\tau-1};x_{i})-\hat{\mu}_{g})^{\top}. The target gradient ∇θℓ​(θτ−1,z∗)\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{\tau-1};z^{*}) is computed directly from the target z∗z^{*} and the observed parameter θτ−1\theta_{\tau-1}.

5 Sequential Privacy Audits with SeMI

The empirical mean experiments (Section 3) establish the sequential advantage of SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*} in an idealized setting. Here, we test whether this advantage yields a tighter audit of real ML models. Hence, we use SeMISGD\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{SGD}} for privacy auditing of DP-SGD.

5.1 A High-probability Lower Bound on ε\varepsilon

SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*} and all the competitors that we consider in this section are of the form 𝒜z∗,τγ​(o1,…,oT)=𝟙​(T>γ)\mathcal{A}^{\gamma}_{z^{*},\tau}(o_{1},\dots,o_{T})=\mathds{1}(T>\gamma) where T=T⁡(o1,…,oT,τ)T=T(o_{1},\dots,o_{T},\tau) is some test statistic and γ\gamma is some threshold. We now explain how to obtain a statistically valid lower bound on ε\varepsilon for an MI test of this form.

We run RR rounds of SeMI game (Algorithm 2) and record the membership indicators B1,…,BRB_{1},\dots,B_{R} and the values of the test statistic T1,…,TRT_{1},\dots,T_{R} instead of the decision of test B^1γ,…,B^Rγ\widehat{B}^{\gamma}_{1},\dots,\widehat{B}^{\gamma}_{R} for a particular choice of γ\gamma. Using the membership indicators and test statistics across the multiple runs, we can estimate the Type-I error α⁡(γ)=α⁡(𝒜z∗,τγ)\alpha(\gamma)=\alpha(\mathcal{A}^{\gamma}_{z^{*},\tau}) and Type-II error β⁡(γ)=β⁡(𝒜z∗,τγ)\beta(\gamma)=\beta(\mathcal{A}^{\gamma}_{z^{*},\tau}) of the MI test for any given threshold γ∈ℝ\gamma\in\mathds{R} as α^R​(γ)=1N0​(R)​∑r=1R𝟙​(Tr>γ)​𝟙​(Br=0)\widehat{\alpha}_{R}(\gamma)=\frac{1}{N_{0}(R)}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\mathds{1}(T_{r}>\gamma)\mathds{1}(B_{r}=0) and β^R​(γ)=1N1​(R)​∑r=1R𝟙​(Tr⩽γ)​𝟙​(Br=1)\widehat{\beta}_{R}(\gamma)=\frac{1}{N_{1}(R)}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\mathds{1}(T_{r}\leqslant\gamma)\mathds{1}(B_{r}=1). Here, Ni​(R)=∑r=1R𝟙​(Br=i)N_{i}(R)=\sum_{r=1}^{R}\mathds{1}(B_{r}=i) (for i∈{0,1}i\in\{0,1\}) denotes the number of times the MI test signals positive and negative memberships. Given ξ>0\xi>0, we introduce two upper confidence bounds on the errors

α¯Rξ​(γ)\displaystyle\overline{\alpha}_{R}^{\xi}(\gamma) =α^R​(γ)+log⁡(ξ/4)2​N0​(R),\displaystyle=\widehat{\alpha}_{R}(\gamma)+\sqrt{\frac{\log(\xi/4)}{2N_{0}(R)}},
β¯Rξ​(γ)\displaystyle\overline{\beta}_{R}^{\xi}(\gamma) =β^R​(γ)+log⁡(ξ/4)2​N1​(R),\displaystyle=\widehat{\beta}_{R}(\gamma)+\sqrt{\frac{\log(\xi/4)}{2N_{1}(R)}},

and define

ε¯Rξ​(δ)=log⁡(maxγ∈ℝ⁡max⁡[1−δ−α¯Rξ​(γ)β¯Rξ​(γ),1−δ−β¯Rξ​(γ)α¯Rξ​(γ)]).\underline{\varepsilon}_{R}^{\xi}(\delta)=\log\left(\max_{\gamma\in\mathbb{R}}\max\left[\frac{1-\delta-\overline{\alpha}_{R}^{\xi}(\gamma)}{\overline{\beta}_{R}^{\xi}(\gamma)},\frac{1-\delta-\overline{\beta}_{R}^{\xi}(\gamma)}{\overline{\alpha}_{R}^{\xi}(\gamma)}\right]\right).
Lemma 5.1.

If the mechanism used in SeMI satisfies (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP, then ℙ⁡(ε⩾ε¯Rξ​(δ))⩾1−ξ\mathbb{P}\left(\varepsilon\geqslant\underline{\varepsilon}_{R}^{\xi}(\delta)\right)\geqslant 1-\xi.

The proof, given in Appendix G, relies on uniform concentration of the empirical CDF of the test statistic, which allows to optimize over γ\gamma. Previous approaches (Nasr et al., 2021) instead built confidence bounds on the errors for each γ\gamma separately and then optimize over γ\gamma, which actually affects the overall statistical accuracy as it requires some union bound on γ\gamma.

5.2 Experiments: Auditing Private Fine-tuning

Experimental Setup. Models are pretrained on a public data split with SGD, then fine-tuned on a private split with DP-SGD (Abadi et al., 2016). We use batch size 64, T=10T=10 updates, and δ=10−4\delta=10^{-4}. The auditor observes the full parameter trajectory (θ0,…,θT)(\theta_{0},\ldots,\theta_{T}) and knows the insertion time τ\tau. For each audit, the target z∗z^{*} is selected from a candidate pool by choosing the sample with highest gradient Mahalanobis distance, estimated from a held-out reference set. We average results over τ∈{1,…,T}\tau\in\{1,\ldots,T\} to assess performance across insertion times; Appendix H.5 shows that selecting the best τ\tau post hoc yields tighter bounds, though how to choose τ\tau a priori for a given architecture remains an open question.

Datasets and Models. We test three model architectures: multinomial logistic regression on Fashion-MNIST (Xiao et al., 2017), a frozen pretrained VGG-16 (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014) with a single trainable layer on CIFAR-10 (Krizhevsky et al., 2009), and a fully connected network (128 hidden units) on Purchase-100 (Shokri et al., 2017).

Hypothesis. The likelihood ratio test SeMISGD\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{SGD}} with known insertion time τ\tau yields tighter privacy lower bounds than heuristic sequential attacks, because it exploits the isolation property to focus on the batch where the target was inserted.

Baselines. We compare against four heuristic attacks from (Jagielski et al., 2023). Delta attacks measure the maximum change in loss across consecutive updates. Delta Diff uses S=maxt⁡(ℓ⁡(θt−1,z∗)−ℓ⁡(θt,z∗))S=\max_{t}(\ell(\theta_{t-1};z^{*})-\ell(\theta_{t};z^{*})) and Delta Ratio uses S=maxt⁡ℓ⁡(θt−1,z∗)/ℓ⁡(θt,z∗)S=\max_{t}\ell(\theta_{t-1};z^{*})/\ell(\theta_{t};z^{*}). The Back-Front attacks measure the total change from initial to final model. Back-Front Diff uses S=ℓ⁡(θ0,z∗)−ℓ⁡(θT,z∗)S=\ell(\theta_{0};z^{*})-\ell(\theta_{T};z^{*}) and Back-Front Ratio uses S=ℓ⁡(θ0,z∗)/ℓ⁡(θT,z∗)S=\ell(\theta_{0};z^{*})/\ell(\theta_{T};z^{*}). All baselines use loss values rather than gradients and are oblivious to τ\tau.

Results. Figure 3 shows εest\varepsilon_{\text{est}} versus ground truth ε\varepsilon across three datasets. On Fashion-MNIST, the hypothesis is supported: SeMISGD\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{SGD}} yields tighter privacy lower bounds than all baselines across the privacy range. On CIFAR-10 and Purchase-100, SeMISGD\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{SGD}} performs as well as or better than baselines, with the clearest gains in low-privacy regimes.

ROC curves in Appendix H.4 show that SeMISGD\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{SGD}} achieves near-perfect discrimination without DP noise and maintains an advantage at low false positive rates under DP-SGD. Appendix H.5 shows that selecting the best fixed insertion time can improve the tightness of the audit compared to averaging over τ\tau.

6 Discussion and Future Works

We derived the optimal membership inference test for sequential model observations and characterized its power in closed form for Gaussian data under the empirical mean mechanism. The isolation property shows that sequential access recovers the batch statistic at insertion time, eliminating the dilution effect that weakens static tests as training data accumulates. We designed tests for three insertion time scenarios: known, uniformly random, and unknown. The extension to SGD relies on batch gradient Gaussianity. Despite this strong assumption, experiments on DP-SGD fine-tuning show that SeMISGD\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{SGD}} yields tighter privacy lower bounds than heuristic baselines, with the strongest gains in low-privacy regimes.

An important aspect of model updates is distribution shift. Though we have shown that SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*} is robust to distribution shifts, it would be important to quantify the impact of distribution shift when the insertion time is unknown and chosen from a distribution by the Crafter. It is also interesting to study whether a Crafter can choose a distribution of insertion time that avoids detection by a privacy-preserving mechanism. Finally, like most of the tight privacy auditing literature, our audits of SGD and DP-SGD are white-box while the SeMI framework can generalize to black-box settings, i.e., when we do not have access to the gradients and can only query the models at each step to obtain the corresponding outputs. It will be interesting and practically useful to extend the optimal sequential MI tests and develop tight auditing mechanisms to the black-box setting.

Appendix A Proofs for the Optimal Test

We consider TT batches of size nn drawn from 𝒟=𝒩⁡(μ,σ2)\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}) with known parameters (μ,σ2)(\mu,\sigma^{2}). The target z∗∈ℝz^{*}\in\mathbb{R} is fixed. We test 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}} against 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}}, where 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}} is the null hypothesis that z∗z^{*} is not in DτD_{\tau} and 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}} is the alternative hypothesis that z∗z^{*} is in DτD_{\tau}. The insertion time τ∈{1,…,T}\tau\in\{1,\ldots,T\} is assumed known.

Notation. We write X¯t=1n​∑k=1nXt,k\bar{X}_{t}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}X_{t,k} for the batch mean and μ^t=1t​n​∑j=1t∑k=1nXj,k\hat{\mu}_{t}=\frac{1}{tn}\sum_{j=1}^{t}\sum_{k=1}^{n}X_{j,k} for the cumulative empirical mean, which satisfies the recursion μ^t=t−1t​μ^t−1+1t​X¯t\hat{\mu}_{t}=\frac{t-1}{t}\hat{\mu}_{t-1}+\frac{1}{t}\bar{X}_{t}.

A.1 Proof of Lemma 3.2

See 3.2

Proof.

The likelihood ratio factorizes using the chain rule for conditional densities:

LRτ=p⁡(μ^1,…,μ^T∣𝐇𝟏τ)p⁡(μ^1,…,μ^T∣𝐇𝟎)=∏t=1Tp⁡(μ^t∣μ^1,…,μ^t−1,𝐇𝟏τ)p⁡(μ^t∣μ^1,…,μ^t−1,𝐇𝟎).\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}=\frac{p(\hat{\mu}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\mu}_{T}\mid\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}})}{p(\hat{\mu}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\mu}_{T}\mid\mathbf{H_{0}})}=\prod_{t=1}^{T}\frac{p(\hat{\mu}_{t}\mid\hat{\mu}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\mu}_{t-1},\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}})}{p(\hat{\mu}_{t}\mid\hat{\mu}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\mu}_{t-1},\mathbf{H_{0}})}.

The recursive relation μ^t=t−1t​μ^t−1+1t​X¯t\hat{\mu}_{t}=\frac{t-1}{t}\hat{\mu}_{t-1}+\frac{1}{t}\bar{X}_{t} implies that, given μ^t−1\hat{\mu}_{t-1}, the distribution of μ^t\hat{\mu}_{t} depends only on the distribution of the new batch mean X¯t\bar{X}_{t}. Earlier observations μ^1,…,μ^t−2\hat{\mu}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\mu}_{t-2} provide no additional information once μ^t−1\hat{\mu}_{t-1} is known.

Terms for t≠τt\neq\tau cancel. For t<τt<\tau, the target z∗z^{*} has not yet been inserted into any batch. Under both 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}} and 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}}, all samples in batches D1,…,DtD_{1},\ldots,D_{t} are drawn i.i.d. from 𝒟\mathcal{D}. The conditional distribution of μ^t\hat{\mu}_{t} given μ^t−1\hat{\mu}_{t-1} is therefore identical under both hypotheses, and the corresponding factor in the product equals 1.

For t>τt>\tau, the batch DtD_{t} contains no target sample under either hypothesis. Although the effect of z∗z^{*} is present in μ^t−1\hat{\mu}_{t-1} under 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}}, conditioning on μ^t−1\hat{\mu}_{t-1} absorbs this effect. The new batch X¯t\bar{X}_{t} is drawn from 𝒩⁡(μ,σ2/n)\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}/n) under both hypotheses, so the conditional distributions of μ^t\hat{\mu}_{t} given μ^t−1\hat{\mu}_{t-1} are again identical. These factors also equal 1.

The only factor that differs between the two hypotheses is the one at t=τt=\tau, where the batch DτD_{\tau} contains z∗z^{*} under 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}} but not under 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}. ∎

A.2 Proof of Theorem 3.4

See 3.4

Proof.

We derive the log likelihood ratio from the conditional distributions at time τ\tau.

Conditional distributions. From the main text, the conditional distributions are:

μ^τ|μ^τ−1,𝐇𝟎\displaystyle\hat{\mu}_{\tau}\mid\hat{\mu}_{\tau-1},\mathbf{H_{0}} ∼𝒩⁡(m0,v0)\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}\left(m_{0},v_{0}\right)
μ^τ|μ^τ−1,𝐇𝟏τ\displaystyle\hat{\mu}_{\tau}\mid\hat{\mu}_{\tau-1},\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}} ∼𝒩⁡(m1,v1)\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}\left(m_{1},v_{1}\right)

where

m0\displaystyle m_{0} =τ−1τ​μ^τ−1+μτ,\displaystyle=\frac{\tau-1}{\tau}\hat{\mu}_{\tau-1}+\frac{\mu}{\tau}, v0\displaystyle v_{0} =σ2τ2​n,\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\tau^{2}n},
m1\displaystyle m_{1} =τ−1τ​μ^τ−1+(n−1)​μ+z∗τ​n,\displaystyle=\frac{\tau-1}{\tau}\hat{\mu}_{\tau-1}+\frac{(n-1)\mu+z^{*}}{\tau n}, v1\displaystyle v_{1} =(n−1)​σ2τ2​n2.\displaystyle=\frac{(n-1)\sigma^{2}}{\tau^{2}n^{2}}.

Log likelihood ratio. Let N=μ^τ−m0N=\hat{\mu}_{\tau}-m_{0}. The log likelihood ratio between two Gaussians is:

log⁡LRτ=−12​log⁡(v1v0)+N22​v0−(N−(m1−m0))22​v1.\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}=-\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{v_{1}}{v_{0}}\right)+\frac{N^{2}}{2v_{0}}-\frac{(N-(m_{1}-m_{0}))^{2}}{2v_{1}}.

Expanding (N−(m1−m0))2(N-(m_{1}-m_{0}))^{2}:

log⁡LRτ\displaystyle\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau} =−12​log⁡(v1v0)+N2​(12​v0−12​v1)+N⁡(m1−m0)v1−(m1−m0)22​v1.\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{v_{1}}{v_{0}}\right)+N^{2}\left(\frac{1}{2v_{0}}-\frac{1}{2v_{1}}\right)+\frac{N(m_{1}-m_{0})}{v_{1}}-\frac{(m_{1}-m_{0})^{2}}{2v_{1}}.

Variance ratio and mean difference. The variance ratio is:

v1v0=(n−1)​σ2/(τ2​n2)σ2/(τ2​n)=n−1n.\frac{v_{1}}{v_{0}}=\frac{(n-1)\sigma^{2}/(\tau^{2}n^{2})}{\sigma^{2}/(\tau^{2}n)}=\frac{n-1}{n}.

The mean difference is:

m1−m0=(n−1)​μ+z∗τ​n−μτ=(n−1)​μ+z∗−n​μτ​n=z∗−μτ​n.m_{1}-m_{0}=\frac{(n-1)\mu+z^{*}}{\tau n}-\frac{\mu}{\tau}=\frac{(n-1)\mu+z^{*}-n\mu}{\tau n}=\frac{z^{*}-\mu}{\tau n}.

Simplification. Using N=1τ​(X¯τ−μ)N=\frac{1}{\tau}(\bar{X}_{\tau}-\mu) and computing the coefficients:

12​v0−12​v1\displaystyle\frac{1}{2v_{0}}-\frac{1}{2v_{1}} =τ2​n2​σ2−τ2​n22​(n−1)​σ2=−τ2​n2​(n−1)​σ2,\displaystyle=\frac{\tau^{2}n}{2\sigma^{2}}-\frac{\tau^{2}n^{2}}{2(n-1)\sigma^{2}}=-\frac{\tau^{2}n}{2(n-1)\sigma^{2}},
m1−m0v1\displaystyle\frac{m_{1}-m_{0}}{v_{1}} =(z∗−μ)​τ​n(n−1)​σ2,\displaystyle=\frac{(z^{*}-\mu)\tau n}{(n-1)\sigma^{2}},
(m1−m0)22​v1\displaystyle\frac{(m_{1}-m_{0})^{2}}{2v_{1}} =(z∗−μ)22​(n−1)​σ2.\displaystyle=\frac{(z^{*}-\mu)^{2}}{2(n-1)\sigma^{2}}.

Substituting N​τ=X¯τ−μN\tau=\bar{X}_{\tau}-\mu, the τ\tau factors cancel in the quadratic and linear terms, yielding:

log⁡LRτ=−12​log⁡(n−1n)−n2​(n−1)​σ2​(X¯τ−μ)2+(z∗−μ)​n(n−1)​σ2​(X¯τ−μ)−(z∗−μ)22​(n−1)​σ2.\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}=-\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)-\frac{n}{2(n-1)\sigma^{2}}(\bar{X}_{\tau}-\mu)^{2}+\frac{(z^{*}-\mu)n}{(n-1)\sigma^{2}}(\bar{X}_{\tau}-\mu)-\frac{(z^{*}-\mu)^{2}}{2(n-1)\sigma^{2}}.

∎

A.3 Proof of Lemma 3.5

See 3.5

Proof.

The test statistic has the quadratic form log⁡LRτ=c0+c1​N+c2​N2\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}=c_{0}+c_{1}N+c_{2}N^{2} where c2<0c_{2}<0.

The condition log⁡LRτ⩾γ\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}\geqslant\gamma is equivalent to c2​N2+c1​N+(c0−γ)⩾0c_{2}N^{2}+c_{1}N+(c_{0}-\gamma)\geqslant 0. Since c2<0c_{2}<0, this downward-opening parabola is non-negative only when NN lies between its two roots (if they exist).

The discriminant of the quadratic is:

Δ=c12−4​c2​(c0−γ)=τ2​nσ2​(n−1)​[(z∗−μ)2σ2−log⁡(n−1n)−2​γ].\Delta=c_{1}^{2}-4c_{2}(c_{0}-\gamma)=\frac{\tau^{2}n}{\sigma^{2}(n-1)}\left[\frac{(z^{*}-\mu)^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}-\log\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)-2\gamma\right].

Case 1: If Δ<0\Delta<0, the parabola never reaches zero, so α=0\alpha=0. This occurs when γ>γmax\gamma>\gamma_{\max}.

Case 2: For Δ⩾0\Delta\geqslant 0, the roots are:

N1,2=z∗−μτ∓σ​n−1τ​n​(z∗−μ)2σ2−log⁡(n−1n)−2​γ.N_{1,2}=\frac{z^{*}-\mu}{\tau}\mp\frac{\sigma\sqrt{n-1}}{\tau\sqrt{n}}\sqrt{\frac{(z^{*}-\mu)^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}-\log\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)-2\gamma}.

Under 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}, N∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2/(τ2​n))N\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}/(\tau^{2}n)). The Type I error is:

α⁡(γ)=P0​(N1⩽N⩽N2)=Φ⁡(N2σ/(τ​n))−Φ⁡(N1σ/(τ​n)).\alpha(\gamma)=P_{0}(N_{1}\leqslant N\leqslant N_{2})=\Phi\left(\frac{N_{2}}{\sigma/(\tau\sqrt{n})}\right)-\Phi\left(\frac{N_{1}}{\sigma/(\tau\sqrt{n})}\right).

Substituting the expressions for N1N_{1} and N2N_{2} and simplifying (noting that τ\tau cancels) yields the stated formula with a=(z∗−μ)​nσa=\frac{(z^{*}-\mu)\sqrt{n}}{\sigma} and b⁡(γ)=n−1​(z∗−μ)2σ2−log⁡(n−1n)−2​γb(\gamma)=\sqrt{n-1}\sqrt{\frac{(z^{*}-\mu)^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}-\log\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)-2\gamma}. ∎

A.4 Proof of Lemma 3.6

See 3.6

Proof.

The Type II error is β⁡(γ)=P1​(log⁡LRτ<γ)=P1​(N<N1)+P1​(N>N2)\beta(\gamma)=P_{1}(\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}<\gamma)=P_{1}(N<N_{1})+P_{1}(N>N_{2}).

Under 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}}, the batch mean is X¯τ∼𝒩⁡((n−1)​μ+z∗n,(n−1)​σ2n2)\bar{X}_{\tau}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{(n-1)\mu+z^{*}}{n},\frac{(n-1)\sigma^{2}}{n^{2}}\right). Therefore:

N=1τ​(X¯τ−μ)∼𝒩⁡(z∗−μτ​n,(n−1)​σ2τ2​n2).N=\frac{1}{\tau}(\bar{X}_{\tau}-\mu)\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{z^{*}-\mu}{\tau n},\frac{(n-1)\sigma^{2}}{\tau^{2}n^{2}}\right).

Let μ1=z∗−μτ​n\mu_{1}=\frac{z^{*}-\mu}{\tau n} and σ1=σ​n−1τ​n\sigma_{1}=\frac{\sigma\sqrt{n-1}}{\tau n}. Then:

β⁡(γ)=Φ⁡(N1−μ1σ1)+Φ⁡(−(N2−μ1)σ1).\beta(\gamma)=\Phi\left(\frac{N_{1}-\mu_{1}}{\sigma_{1}}\right)+\Phi\left(\frac{-(N_{2}-\mu_{1})}{\sigma_{1}}\right).

From the expressions for N1,2N_{1,2} and after algebraic simplification:

N1,2−μ1σ1=(z∗−μ)​n−1σ∓n​(z∗−μ)2σ2−log⁡(n−1n)−2​γ.\displaystyle\frac{N_{1,2}-\mu_{1}}{\sigma_{1}}=\frac{(z^{*}-\mu)\sqrt{n-1}}{\sigma}\mp\sqrt{n}\sqrt{\frac{(z^{*}-\mu)^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}-\log\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)-2\gamma}.

This yields the stated formula. ∎

A.5 Proof of Lemma 3.7

See 3.7

Proof.

The proof follows the same structure as Lemma 3.5, with nn replaced by n​TnT throughout.

For the single-observation case, the test statistic is log⁡LR=c0(T)+c1(T)​W+c2(T)​W2\log\mathrm{LR}=c_{0}^{(T)}+c_{1}^{(T)}W+c_{2}^{(T)}W^{2} where W=μ^T−μW=\hat{\mu}_{T}-\mu and:

c0(T)\displaystyle c_{0}^{(T)} =−12​log⁡(n​T−1n​T)−(z∗−μ)22​(n​T−1)​σ2,\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{nT-1}{nT}\right)-\frac{(z^{*}-\mu)^{2}}{2(nT-1)\sigma^{2}},
c1(T)\displaystyle c_{1}^{(T)} =n​T​(z∗−μ)(n​T−1)​σ2,\displaystyle=\frac{nT(z^{*}-\mu)}{(nT-1)\sigma^{2}},
c2(T)\displaystyle c_{2}^{(T)} =−n​T2​(n​T−1)​σ2.\displaystyle=-\frac{nT}{2(nT-1)\sigma^{2}}.

The discriminant is:

Δ=n​Tσ2​(n​T−1)​[(z∗−μ)2σ2−log⁡(n​T−1n​T)−2​γ].\Delta=\frac{nT}{\sigma^{2}(nT-1)}\left[\frac{(z^{*}-\mu)^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}-\log\left(\frac{nT-1}{nT}\right)-2\gamma\right].

For Δ⩾0\Delta\geqslant 0, the roots are:

W1,2=z∗−μn​T∓σ​n​T−1n​T​(z∗−μ)2σ2−log⁡(n​T−1n​T)−2​γ.W_{1,2}=\frac{z^{*}-\mu}{nT}\mp\frac{\sigma\sqrt{nT-1}}{nT}\sqrt{\frac{(z^{*}-\mu)^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}-\log\left(\frac{nT-1}{nT}\right)-2\gamma}.

Under 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}, W∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2/(n​T))W\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}/(nT)), giving the stated formula. ∎

A.6 Proof of Lemma 3.8

See 3.8

Proof.

Under 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}}, one sample among n​TnT is replaced by z∗z^{*}:

W=μ^T−μ∼𝒩⁡(z∗−μn​T,(n​T−1)​σ2(n​T)2).W=\hat{\mu}_{T}-\mu\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{z^{*}-\mu}{nT},\frac{(nT-1)\sigma^{2}}{(nT)^{2}}\right).

The Type II error β⁡(γ)=P1​(W<W1)+P1​(W>W2)\beta(\gamma)=P_{1}(W<W_{1})+P_{1}(W>W_{2}) follows by the same calculation as Lemma 3.6, with nn replaced by n​TnT. ∎

Appendix B Multivariate Gaussian Extension

We extend the sequential membership inference approach to the multivariate Gaussian setting where datapoints lie in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. We consider TT batches of size nn drawn from 𝒟=𝒩⁡(𝝁,𝚺)\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) where 𝝁∈ℝd\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and 𝚺∈ℝd×d\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is positive definite and known. The target 𝐳∗∈ℝd\mathbf{z}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and τ\tau are known. We test 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}} versus 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}} as defined in (4).

Notation. Bold symbols denote vectors (𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}) and matrices (𝚺∈ℝd×d\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}). The Mahalanobis distance is ‖𝐱‖𝚺=𝐱⊤​𝚺−1​𝐱\|\mathbf{x}\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}=\sqrt{\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x}}.

B.1 Conditional Distributions

The recursive relation 𝝁^t=t−1t​𝝁^t−1+1t​𝐗¯t\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{t}=\frac{t-1}{t}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{t-1}+\frac{1}{t}\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{t} extends naturally.

Lemma B.1 (Multivariate Conditional Distributions).

The conditional distributions at time τ\tau are:

𝝁^τ|𝝁^τ−1,𝐇𝟎\displaystyle\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\tau}\mid\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\tau-1},\mathbf{H_{0}} ∼𝒩⁡(τ−1τ​𝝁^τ−1+𝝁τ,𝚺τ2​n),\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{\tau-1}{\tau}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\tau-1}+\frac{\boldsymbol{\mu}}{\tau},\frac{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\tau^{2}n}\right),
𝝁^τ|𝝁^τ−1,𝐇𝟏τ\displaystyle\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\tau}\mid\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\tau-1},\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}} ∼𝒩⁡(τ−1τ​𝝁^τ−1+(n−1)​𝝁+𝐳∗τ​n,(n−1)​𝚺τ2​n2).\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{\tau-1}{\tau}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\tau-1}+\frac{(n-1)\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbf{z}^{*}}{\tau n},\frac{(n-1)\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\tau^{2}n^{2}}\right).
Proof.

Batch mean distributions. Under 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}, the batch mean is 𝐗¯τ∼𝒩⁡(𝝁,𝚺/n)\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{\tau}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}/n).

Under 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}}, the batch contains (n−1)(n-1) samples from 𝒟\mathcal{D} plus 𝐳∗\mathbf{z}^{*}:

𝐗¯τ=1n​[(n−1)​𝝁sample+𝐳∗]\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{\tau}=\frac{1}{n}\left[(n-1)\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{sample}}+\mathbf{z}^{*}\right]

where 𝝁sample∼𝒩⁡(𝝁,𝚺/(n−1))\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{sample}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}/(n-1)). The result follows.

The recursion 𝝁^τ=τ−1τ​𝝁^τ−1+1τ​𝐗¯τ\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\tau}=\frac{\tau-1}{\tau}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\tau-1}+\frac{1}{\tau}\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{\tau} is an affine transformation, yielding the stated conditional distributions. ∎

B.2 Log Likelihood Ratio

Theorem B.2 (Multivariate Log Likelihood Ratio).

Define 𝐍τ=τ⁡(𝛍^τ−τ−1τ​𝛍^τ−1−𝛍τ)=𝐗¯τ−𝛍\mathbf{N_{\tau}}=\tau(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\tau}-\frac{\tau-1}{\tau}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\tau-1}-\frac{\boldsymbol{\mu}}{\tau})=\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{\tau}-\boldsymbol{\mu}. The log likelihood ratio is:

log⁡LRτ\displaystyle\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau} =−d2​log⁡(n−1n)−n2​(n−1)​𝐍τ⊤​𝚺−1​𝐍τ\displaystyle=-\frac{d}{2}\log\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)-\frac{n}{2(n-1)}\mathbf{N_{\tau}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{N_{\tau}}
+nn−1​𝐍τ⊤​𝚺−1​(𝐳∗−𝝁)−(𝐳∗−𝝁)⊤​𝚺−1​(𝐳∗−𝝁)2​(n−1).\displaystyle\quad+\frac{n}{n-1}\mathbf{N_{\tau}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{z}^{*}-\boldsymbol{\mu})-\frac{(\mathbf{z}^{*}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{z}^{*}-\boldsymbol{\mu})}{2(n-1)}.

Conditional parameters. Let 𝐦0,𝐦1\mathbf{m}_{0},\mathbf{m}_{1} be the conditional means and 𝐕0=𝚺τ2​n\mathbf{V}_{0}=\frac{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\tau^{2}n}, 𝐕1=(n−1)​𝚺τ2​n2\mathbf{V}_{1}=\frac{(n-1)\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\tau^{2}n^{2}} the conditional covariances.

Covariance ratio and mean difference. We have 𝐕1=n−1n​𝐕0\mathbf{V}_{1}=\frac{n-1}{n}\mathbf{V}_{0}, so det(𝐕1)=(n−1n)d​det(𝐕0)\det(\mathbf{V}_{1})=\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)^{d}\det(\mathbf{V}_{0}) and 𝐕1−1=nn−1​𝐕0−1\mathbf{V}_{1}^{-1}=\frac{n}{n-1}\mathbf{V}_{0}^{-1}. The mean difference is:

𝐦1−𝐦0=(n−1)​𝝁+𝐳∗τ​n−𝝁τ=𝐳∗−𝝁τ​n.\mathbf{m}_{1}-\mathbf{m}_{0}=\frac{(n-1)\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbf{z}^{*}}{\tau n}-\frac{\boldsymbol{\mu}}{\tau}=\frac{\mathbf{z}^{*}-\boldsymbol{\mu}}{\tau n}.

Log likelihood ratio. The multivariate Gaussian log likelihood ratio is:

log⁡LRτ=−12​log⁡det(𝐕1)det(𝐕0)+12​𝐋τ⊤​𝐕0−1​𝐋τ−12​(𝐋τ−(𝐦1−𝐦0))⊤​𝐕1−1​(𝐋τ−(𝐦1−𝐦0))\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}=-\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{\det(\mathbf{V}_{1})}{\det(\mathbf{V}_{0})}+\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{L_{\tau}}^{\top}\mathbf{V}_{0}^{-1}\mathbf{L_{\tau}}-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{L_{\tau}}-(\mathbf{m}_{1}-\mathbf{m}_{0}))^{\top}\mathbf{V}_{1}^{-1}(\mathbf{L_{\tau}}-(\mathbf{m}_{1}-\mathbf{m}_{0}))

where 𝐋τ=𝝁^τ−𝐦0=1τ​𝐍τ\mathbf{L_{\tau}}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\tau}-\mathbf{m}_{0}=\frac{1}{\tau}\mathbf{N_{\tau}}. The determinant term gives −d2​log⁡(n−1n)-\frac{d}{2}\log\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right). Expanding the quadratic terms with 𝐕0−1=τ2​n​𝚺−1\mathbf{V}_{0}^{-1}=\tau^{2}n\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} and simplifying yields the stated result. ∎

Corollary B.3 (Quadratic Form).

The log likelihood ratio has the form log⁡LRτ=c0+𝐜1⊤​𝐍τ+𝐍τ⊤​𝐂2​𝐍τ\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}=c_{0}+\mathbf{c}_{1}^{\top}\mathbf{N_{\tau}}+\mathbf{N_{\tau}}^{\top}\mathbf{C}_{2}\mathbf{N_{\tau}} where:
