and m∗=(𝐳∗−𝛍)⊤​𝚺−1​(𝐳∗−𝛍)m^{*}=(\mathbf{z}^{*}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{z}^{*}-\boldsymbol{\mu}) is the squared Mahalanobis distance.

B.3 Type I and II Error Analysis

Lemma B.4 (Distributions of the Test Statistic).

Under 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}: 𝐍τ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝚺n)\mathbf{N_{\tau}}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{0},\frac{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{n}\right).

Under 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}}: 𝐍τ∼𝒩⁡(𝐳∗−𝛍n,(n−1)​𝚺n2)\mathbf{N_{\tau}}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{\mathbf{z}^{*}-\boldsymbol{\mu}}{n},\frac{(n-1)\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{n^{2}}\right).

Lemma B.5 (Type I Error Analysis - Diagonal Case).

For the log likelihood ratio test with threshold γ\gamma in the multivariate Gaussian case with diagonal covariance 𝚺=diag⁡(σ12,…,σd2)\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{2},\ldots,\sigma_{d}^{2}), let:

γmax=12​[m∗−d​log⁡(n−1n)]\gamma_{\max}=\frac{1}{2}\left[m^{*}-d\log\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)\right]

where m∗=∑j=1d(zj∗−μj)2σj2m^{*}=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{(z^{*}_{j}-\mu_{j})^{2}}{\sigma_{j}^{2}} is the squared Mahalanobis distance. For γ⩽γmax\gamma\leqslant\gamma_{\max}, the Type I error is:

α⁡(γ)=ℙ0​(‖𝐔‖𝚺−12⩽R2​(γ))\alpha(\gamma)=\mathbb{P}_{0}\left(\|\mathbf{U}\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}}^{2}\leqslant R^{2}(\gamma)\right)

where 𝐔∼𝒩⁡(−(𝐳∗−𝛍),𝚺n)\mathbf{U}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(-(\mathbf{z}^{*}-\boldsymbol{\mu}),\frac{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{n}\right) and R2​(γ)=2​(n−1)n​[n2​m∗2−γ−d2​log⁡(n−1n)]R^{2}(\gamma)=\frac{2(n-1)}{n}\left[\frac{n^{2}m^{*}}{2}-\gamma-\frac{d}{2}\log\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)\right].

Proof.

With diagonal covariance, the log likelihood ratio sums over dimensions: log⁡LRτ=∑j=1dlog⁡LRτ,j\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau,j}. The sum can be written as log⁡LRτ=𝐍τ⊤​𝐂2​𝐍τ+𝐜1⊤​𝐍τ+c0\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}=\mathbf{N_{\tau}}^{\top}\mathbf{C}_{2}\mathbf{N_{\tau}}+\mathbf{c}_{1}^{\top}\mathbf{N_{\tau}}+c_{0} with diagonal 𝐂2\mathbf{C}_{2}.

Substituting the coefficients from Corollary B.3 (adapted for diagonal 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma}), we complete the square. Let 𝐌τ=𝐍τ−(𝐳∗−𝝁)\mathbf{M_{\tau}}=\mathbf{N_{\tau}}-(\mathbf{z}^{*}-\boldsymbol{\mu}). Under 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}, 𝐍τ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝚺/n)\mathbf{N_{\tau}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}/n), so 𝐌τ∼𝒩⁡(−(𝐳∗−𝝁),𝚺/n)\mathbf{M_{\tau}}\sim\mathcal{N}(-(\mathbf{z}^{*}-\boldsymbol{\mu}),\boldsymbol{\Sigma}/n).

The condition log⁡LRτ⩾γ\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}\geqslant\gamma transforms to:

𝐌τ⊤​𝐂2​𝐌τ⩾γ−c0+14​𝐜1⊤​𝐂2−1​𝐜1.\mathbf{M_{\tau}}^{\top}\mathbf{C}_{2}\mathbf{M_{\tau}}\geqslant\gamma-c_{0}+\frac{1}{4}\mathbf{c}_{1}^{\top}\mathbf{C}_{2}^{-1}\mathbf{c}_{1}.

Substituting the specific values for c0,𝐜1,𝐂2c_{0},\mathbf{c}_{1},\mathbf{C}_{2}, the RHS simplifies to γ+d2​log⁡(n−1n)−n2​m∗2\gamma+\frac{d}{2}\log\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)-\frac{n^{2}m^{*}}{2}.

Since 𝐂2=−n2​(n−1)​𝚺−1\mathbf{C}_{2}=-\frac{n}{2(n-1)}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} is negative definite, the inequality reverses:

𝐌τ⊤​𝚺−1​𝐌τ⩽−2​(n−1)n​[γ+d2​log⁡(n−1n)−n2​m∗2].\mathbf{M_{\tau}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{M_{\tau}}\leqslant-\frac{2(n-1)}{n}\left[\gamma+\frac{d}{2}\log\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)-\frac{n^{2}m^{*}}{2}\right].

Letting 𝐔=𝐌τ\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{M_{\tau}}, the result follows. The probability is the mass of a shifted Gaussian within an ellipsoid defined by the Mahalanobis distance. ∎

Corollary B.6 (Explicit Type I Error).

For diagonal covariance 𝚺=diag⁡(σ12,…,σd2)\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{2},\ldots,\sigma_{d}^{2}), the Type I error is:

α⁡(γ)=Fχd2​(n​m∗)​(n​R2​(γ))\alpha(\gamma)=F_{\chi^{2}_{d}(nm^{*})}\left(n\,R^{2}(\gamma)\right)

where Fχd2​(λ)F_{\chi^{2}_{d}(\lambda)} is the CDF of the non-central chi-squared distribution with dd degrees of freedom and non-centrality parameter λ=n​m∗\lambda=nm^{*}, and R2​(γ)R^{2}(\gamma) is defined as in Lemma 3.5.

Proof.

For diagonal 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma}, the squared Mahalanobis norm decomposes as ‖𝐔‖𝚺−12=∑j=1dUj2/σj2\|\mathbf{U}\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}}^{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{d}U_{j}^{2}/\sigma_{j}^{2}. Each component Uj∼𝒩⁡(−(zj∗−μj),σj2/n)U_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(-(z_{j}^{*}-\mu_{j}),\sigma_{j}^{2}/n), so the standardized variable Wj=nUj/σj∼𝒩(−n(zj∗−μj)/σj,1)W_{j}=\sqrt{n}U_{j}/\sigma_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(-\sqrt{n}(z_{j}^{*}-\mu_{j})/\sigma_{j},1).

The sum ∑j=1dWj2=n​‖𝐔‖𝚺−12\sum_{j=1}^{d}W_{j}^{2}=n\|\mathbf{U}\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}}^{2} follows a non-central chi-squared distribution with dd degrees of freedom and non-centrality parameter λ=∑j=1dn​(zj∗−μj)2/σj2=n​m∗\lambda=\sum_{j=1}^{d}n(z_{j}^{*}-\mu_{j})^{2}/\sigma_{j}^{2}=nm^{*}. ∎

Appendix C Robustness to Distribution Shift

We consider the setting where each batch may be drawn from a different distribution: Dt∼𝒩⁡(μt,σt2)D_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{t},\sigma_{t}^{2}) for t=1,…,Tt=1,\ldots,T. The target z∗∈ℝz^{*}\in\mathbb{R} and the insertion time τ\tau are fixed. We test 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}} versus 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}}.

Notation. Parameters (μt,σt2)(\mu_{t},\sigma_{t}^{2}) may vary with tt, but only (μτ,στ2)(\mu_{\tau},\sigma_{\tau}^{2}) at the insertion time affect the test.

C.1 Main Result

Theorem C.1 (Robustness to Distribution Shift).

The likelihood ratio test for 𝐇𝟎:z∗∉Dτ\mathbf{H_{0}}:z^{*}\notin D_{\tau} versus 𝐇𝟏τ:z∗∈Dτ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}}:z^{*}\in D_{\tau} depends only on (μτ,στ2)(\mu_{\tau},\sigma_{\tau}^{2}). The distributions of batches DtD_{t} for t≠τt\neq\tau do not affect the test.

Proof.

Likelihood ratio decomposition. The cumulative empirical mean satisfies μ^t=t−1t​μ^t−1+1t​X¯t\hat{\mu}_{t}=\frac{t-1}{t}\hat{\mu}_{t-1}+\frac{1}{t}\bar{X}_{t}. The likelihood ratio decomposes as:

LR=∏t=1Tp⁡(μ^t∣μ^t−1,𝐇𝟏τ)p⁡(μ^t∣μ^t−1,𝐇𝟎).\mathrm{LR}=\prod_{t=1}^{T}\frac{p(\hat{\mu}_{t}\mid\hat{\mu}_{t-1},\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}})}{p(\hat{\mu}_{t}\mid\hat{\mu}_{t-1},\mathbf{H_{0}})}.

Terms for t≠τt\neq\tau cancel. For t<τt<\tau, the target has not been inserted. Under both hypotheses, batch DtD_{t} is drawn from 𝒩⁡(μt,σt2)\mathcal{N}(\mu_{t},\sigma_{t}^{2}). The conditional distributions of μ^t\hat{\mu}_{t} given μ^t−1\hat{\mu}_{t-1} are identical under both hypotheses, so the corresponding factor equals 1.

For t>τt>\tau, batch DtD_{t} contains no target under either hypothesis. Although the effect of z∗z^{*} is present in μ^t−1\hat{\mu}_{t-1} under 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}}, conditioning on μ^t−1\hat{\mu}_{t-1} absorbs this effect. The batch X¯t\bar{X}_{t} is drawn from 𝒩⁡(μt,σt2/n)\mathcal{N}(\mu_{t},\sigma_{t}^{2}/n) under both hypotheses, so the conditional distributions of μ^t\hat{\mu}_{t} given μ^t−1\hat{\mu}_{t-1} are identical. These factors also equal 1.

The transition at t=τt=\tau. The only factor that differs is at t=τt=\tau, where the conditional distributions are:

μ^τ|μ^τ−1,𝐇𝟎\displaystyle\hat{\mu}_{\tau}\mid\hat{\mu}_{\tau-1},\mathbf{H_{0}} ∼𝒩⁡(τ−1τ​μ^τ−1+μττ,στ2τ2​n),\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{\tau-1}{\tau}\hat{\mu}_{\tau-1}+\frac{\mu_{\tau}}{\tau},\frac{\sigma_{\tau}^{2}}{\tau^{2}n}\right),
μ^τ|μ^τ−1,𝐇𝟏τ\displaystyle\hat{\mu}_{\tau}\mid\hat{\mu}_{\tau-1},\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}} ∼𝒩⁡(τ−1τ​μ^τ−1+(n−1)​μτ+z∗τ​n,(n−1)​στ2τ2​n2).\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{\tau-1}{\tau}\hat{\mu}_{\tau-1}+\frac{(n-1)\mu_{\tau}+z^{*}}{\tau n},\frac{(n-1)\sigma_{\tau}^{2}}{\tau^{2}n^{2}}\right).

These expressions involve only (μτ,στ2)(\mu_{\tau},\sigma_{\tau}^{2}). The parameters (μt,σt2)(\mu_{t},\sigma_{t}^{2}) for t≠τt\neq\tau do not appear in the likelihood ratio. ∎

Appendix D Proofs for Uniform τ\tau Test

We derive the optimal test for 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}} against 𝐇𝟏~\widetilde{\mathbf{H_{1}}} where τ∼Uniform⁡({1,…,T})\tau\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(\{1,\ldots,T\}). As before, TT batches of size nn are drawn from 𝒟=𝒩⁡(μ,σ2)\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}) with known parameters.

Notation. We write LRt\mathrm{LR}_{t} for the likelihood ratio at time tt (derived in Theorem 3.4) and log⁡LRt\log\mathrm{LR}_{t} for its logarithm. The batch means X¯1,…,X¯T\bar{X}_{1},\ldots,\bar{X}_{T} are independent under both hypotheses.

D.1 Derivation of the Likelihood Ratio

See 3.10

Proof.

Under 𝐇𝟏~\widetilde{\mathbf{H_{1}}}, the insertion time satisfies ℙ⁡(τ=t∣𝐇𝟏~)=1/T\mathbb{P}(\tau=t\mid\widetilde{\mathbf{H_{1}}})=1/T. The marginal likelihood of the observations is:

p(μ^1,…,μ^T∣𝐇𝟏~)=∑t=1Tℙ(τ=t)⋅p(μ^1,…,μ^T∣τ=t,𝐇𝟏~).p(\hat{\mu}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\mu}_{T}\mid\widetilde{\mathbf{H_{1}}})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{P}(\tau=t)\cdot p(\hat{\mu}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\mu}_{T}\mid\tau=t,\widetilde{\mathbf{H_{1}}}).

Conditioned on τ=t\tau=t, the data distribution matches 𝐇𝟏𝐭\mathbf{H_{1}^{t}}:

p(μ^1,…,μ^T∣τ=t,𝐇𝟏~)=p(μ^1,…,μ^T∣𝐇𝟏𝐭).p(\hat{\mu}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\mu}_{T}\mid\tau=t,\widetilde{\mathbf{H_{1}}})=p(\hat{\mu}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\mu}_{T}\mid\mathbf{H_{1}^{t}}).

Dividing by the null likelihood:

LRUnif\displaystyle\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{Unif}} =p⁡(μ^1,…,μ^T∣𝐇𝟏~)p⁡(μ^1,…,μ^T∣𝐇𝟎)=1T​∑t=1Tp⁡(μ^1,…,μ^T∣𝐇𝟏𝐭)p⁡(μ^1,…,μ^T∣𝐇𝟎)=1T​∑t=1TLRt.\displaystyle=\frac{p(\hat{\mu}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\mu}_{T}\mid\widetilde{\mathbf{H_{1}}})}{p(\hat{\mu}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\mu}_{T}\mid\mathbf{H_{0}})}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{p(\hat{\mu}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\mu}_{T}\mid\mathbf{H_{1}^{t}})}{p(\hat{\mu}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\mu}_{T}\mid\mathbf{H_{0}})}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathrm{LR}_{t}.

∎

Each LRt\mathrm{LR}_{t} depends on the data only through X¯t\bar{X}_{t} (by the isolation property), and batch means are independent. The test statistic aggregates evidence across all time steps.

D.2 Log-Sum-Exp Form

Corollary D.1 (Log Likelihood Ratio).

The log likelihood ratio is

log⁡LRUnif=logsumexp⁡(log⁡LR1,…,log⁡LRT)−log⁡T\log\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{Unif}}=\mathrm{logsumexp}(\log\mathrm{LR}_{1},\ldots,\log\mathrm{LR}_{T})-\log T

where logsumexp⁡(x1,…,xT)=log⁡(∑t=1Text)\mathrm{logsumexp}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})=\log\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}e^{x_{t}}\right).

Proof.

Taking the logarithm of Theorem 3.10:

log⁡LRUnif=log⁡(1T​∑t=1TLRt)=log⁡(∑t=1Telog⁡LRt)−log⁡T.\log\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{Unif}}=\log\left(\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathrm{LR}_{t}\right)=\log\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}e^{\log\mathrm{LR}_{t}}\right)-\log T.

∎

The log-sum-exp function is numerically stable: logsumexp⁡(x1,…,xT)=m+log⁡(∑t=1Text−m)\mathrm{logsumexp}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})=m+\log\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}e^{x_{t}-m}\right) where m=maxt⁡xtm=\max_{t}x_{t}.

D.3 Relationship to the GLR Test

Proposition D.2 (Bounds).

The log likelihood ratio satisfies

maxt⁡log⁡LRt−log⁡T⩽log⁡LRUnif⩽maxt⁡log⁡LRt.\max_{t}\log\mathrm{LR}_{t}-\log T\leqslant\log\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{Unif}}\leqslant\max_{t}\log\mathrm{LR}_{t}.
Proof.

Upper bound. Since LRt⩾0\mathrm{LR}_{t}\geqslant 0:

1T​∑t=1TLRt⩽maxt⁡LRt.\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathrm{LR}_{t}\leqslant\max_{t}\mathrm{LR}_{t}.

Lower bound. The average is at least the maximum divided by TT:

1T​∑t=1TLRt⩾1T​maxt​LRt.\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathrm{LR}_{t}\geqslant\frac{1}{T}\max_{t}\mathrm{LR}_{t}.

∎

When one LRt∗\mathrm{LR}_{t^{*}} dominates, log⁡LRUnif≈log⁡LRt∗−log⁡T\log\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{Unif}}\approx\log\mathrm{LR}_{t^{*}}-\log T. When multiple batches contribute comparable evidence, the test accumulates their contributions.

Appendix E Proofs for GLR test

Consider the case where TT batches of size nn are drawn from 𝒟=𝒩⁡(μ,σ2)\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}) with known parameters (μ,σ2)(\mu,\sigma^{2}), but the insertion time is unknown. The target z∗∈ℝz^{*}\in\mathbb{R} is fixed. We test:

𝐇𝟎\displaystyle\mathbf{H_{0}} :All datapoints sampled i.i.d. from ​𝒟\displaystyle:\text{All datapoints sampled i.i.d.\ from }\mathcal{D}
𝐇𝟏~\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbf{H_{1}}} :One sample in ​Dτ​ replaced by ​z∗​ for some unknown ​τ∈{1,…,T}\displaystyle:\text{One sample in }D_{\tau}\text{ replaced by }z^{*}\text{ for some unknown }\tau\in\{1,\ldots,T\}

Notation. We write X¯t\bar{X}_{t} for the batch mean, μ^t\hat{\mu}_{t} for the cumulative empirical mean, and log⁡LRτ\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau} for the log likelihood ratio at time τ\tau. The test statistic for SeMImax\mathrm{SeMI}^{\max} is maxτ⁡log⁡LRτ\max_{\tau}\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}. Single-batch error rates are α0​(γ)=P0​(log⁡LR1⩾γ)\alpha_{0}(\gamma)=P_{0}(\log\mathrm{LR}_{1}\geqslant\gamma) and β0​(γ)=P1​(log⁡LR1<γ)\beta_{0}(\gamma)=P_{1}(\log\mathrm{LR}_{1}<\gamma).

E.1 Independence of Log Likelihood Ratios under 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}

Theorem E.1 (Independence under 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}).

Under 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}, the statistics log⁡LR1,…,log⁡LRT\log\mathrm{LR}_{1},\ldots,\log\mathrm{LR}_{T} are independent and identically distributed.

Proof.

From Theorem 3.4, each log⁡LRτ\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau} depends on the data only through X¯τ−μ\bar{X}_{\tau}-\mu. The coefficients c0c_{0}, c1c_{1}, and c2c_{2} in the quadratic form depend on nn, σ2\sigma^{2}, μ\mu, and z∗z^{*}, but not on τ\tau.

Under 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}, each batch DτD_{\tau} is sampled independently from 𝒩​(μ,σ2)n\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})^{n}. The batch means X¯1,…,X¯T\bar{X}_{1},\ldots,\bar{X}_{T} are therefore independent random variables. Moreover, each X¯τ∼𝒩⁡(μ,σ2/n)\bar{X}_{\tau}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}/n) for all τ∈{1,…,T}\tau\in\{1,\ldots,T\}. Since the log likelihood ratio is a function of X¯τ−μ\bar{X}_{\tau}-\mu with coefficients that do not depend on τ\tau, the statistics log⁡LR1,…,log⁡LRT\log\mathrm{LR}_{1},\ldots,\log\mathrm{LR}_{T} have the same distribution.

The statistics log⁡LRτ\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau} are functions of independent, identically distributed random variables (the batch means), and these functions are identical across τ\tau. Therefore, log⁡LR1,…,log⁡LRT\log\mathrm{LR}_{1},\ldots,\log\mathrm{LR}_{T} are i.i.d. under 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}. ∎

E.2 Proof of Corollary E.2

Corollary E.2 (SeMImax\mathrm{SeMI}^{\max} Type I Error).

The Type I error of SeMImax\mathrm{SeMI}^{\max} with threshold γ\gamma is

αmax​(γ)=1−[1−α0​(γ)]T\alpha_{\max}(\gamma)=1-[1-\alpha_{0}(\gamma)]^{T}

where α0​(γ)\alpha_{0}(\gamma) is the Type I error of the single-batch test from Lemma 3.5.

Proof.

The SeMImax\mathrm{SeMI}^{\max} test rejects when maxτ=1,…,T⁡log⁡LRτ⩾γ\max_{\tau=1,\ldots,T}\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}\geqslant\gamma. The Type I error is:

αmax​(γ)\displaystyle\alpha_{\max}(\gamma) =P0​(SeMImax⩾γ)\displaystyle=P_{0}(\mathrm{SeMI}^{\max}\geqslant\gamma)
=P0​(maxτ=1,…,T⁡log⁡LRτ⩾γ)\displaystyle=P_{0}\left(\max_{\tau=1,\ldots,T}\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}\geqslant\gamma\right)
=1−P0​(log⁡LRτ<γ​ for all ​τ).\displaystyle=1-P_{0}(\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}<\gamma\text{ for all }\tau).

By Theorem E.1, the statistics are independent under 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}:

P0​(log⁡LRτ<γ​ for all ​τ)=∏τ=1TP0​(log⁡LRτ<γ).P_{0}(\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}<\gamma\text{ for all }\tau)=\prod_{\tau=1}^{T}P_{0}(\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}<\gamma).

Since all log⁡LRτ\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau} have the same distribution under 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}:

∏τ=1TP0​(log⁡LRτ<γ)=[P0​(log⁡LR1<γ)]T=[1−α0​(γ)]T.\prod_{\tau=1}^{T}P_{0}(\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}<\gamma)=[P_{0}(\log\mathrm{LR}_{1}<\gamma)]^{T}=[1-\alpha_{0}(\gamma)]^{T}.

Therefore:

αmax​(γ)=1−[1−α0​(γ)]T.\alpha_{\max}(\gamma)=1-[1-\alpha_{0}(\gamma)]^{T}.

∎

To achieve overall Type I error α\alpha, set the threshold γ∗\gamma^{*} such that α0​(γ∗)=1−(1−α)1/T\alpha_{0}(\gamma^{*})=1-(1-\alpha)^{1/T}. For small α\alpha and moderate TT, this approximates the Bonferroni correction α0≈α/T\alpha_{0}\approx\alpha/T.

E.3 Proof of Corollary E.3

Corollary E.3 (SeMImax\mathrm{SeMI}^{\max} Type II Error).

The Type II error of SeMImax\mathrm{SeMI}^{\max}, given true insertion time τ∗\tau^{*}, is

βmax​(γ∣τ∗)=β0​(γ)⋅[1−α0​(γ)]T−1\beta_{\max}(\gamma\mid\tau^{*})=\beta_{0}(\gamma)\cdot[1-\alpha_{0}(\gamma)]^{T-1}

where β0​(γ)\beta_{0}(\gamma) is the Type II error from Lemma 3.6. This does not depend on τ∗\tau^{*}.

Proof.

Under 𝐇𝟏τ∗\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau^{*}}}, the target z∗z^{*} is in batch τ∗\tau^{*}. The Type II error is the probability of failing to reject 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}.

The test fails to reject when all log likelihood ratios are below the threshold:

βmax​(γ∣τ∗)=P1​(SeMImax<γ∣𝐇𝟏τ∗)=P1​(maxτ⁡log⁡LRτ<γ).\beta_{\max}(\gamma\mid\tau^{*})=P_{1}(\mathrm{SeMI}^{\max}<\gamma\mid\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau^{*}}})=P_{1}\left(\max_{\tau}\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}<\gamma\right).

Separating the true insertion time from others:

P1​(maxτ⁡log⁡LRτ<γ)=P1​(log⁡LRτ∗<γ​ and ​maxτ≠τ∗​log⁡LRτ<γ).P_{1}\left(\max_{\tau}\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}<\gamma\right)=P_{1}\left(\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau^{*}}<\gamma\text{ and }\max_{\tau\neq\tau^{*}}\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}<\gamma\right).

Under 𝐇𝟏τ∗\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau^{*}}}, the statistic log⁡LRτ∗\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau^{*}} depends only on batch Dτ∗D_{\tau^{*}}, while log⁡LRτ\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau} for τ≠τ∗\tau\neq\tau^{*} depends only on batch DτD_{\tau}. Since the batches are independent, these statistics are independent:

P1​(log⁡LRτ∗<γ​ and ​maxτ≠τ∗​log⁡LRτ<γ)=P1​(log⁡LRτ∗<γ)⋅P1​(maxτ≠τ∗⁡log⁡LRτ<γ).P_{1}\left(\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau^{*}}<\gamma\text{ and }\max_{\tau\neq\tau^{*}}\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}<\gamma\right)=P_{1}(\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau^{*}}<\gamma)\cdot P_{1}\left(\max_{\tau\neq\tau^{*}}\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}<\gamma\right).

The first factor is β0​(γ)\beta_{0}(\gamma), the Type II error of the single-batch test. For batches τ≠τ∗\tau\neq\tau^{*}, no target is present, so log⁡LRτ\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau} has the null distribution. By the same argument as in Corollary E.2:

P1​(maxτ≠τ∗⁡log⁡LRτ<γ)=[1−α0​(γ)]T−1.P_{1}\left(\max_{\tau\neq\tau^{*}}\log\mathrm{LR}_{\tau}<\gamma\right)=[1-\alpha_{0}(\gamma)]^{T-1}.

Therefore:

βmax​(γ∣τ∗)=β0​(γ)⋅[1−α0​(γ)]T−1.\beta_{\max}(\gamma\mid\tau^{*})=\beta_{0}(\gamma)\cdot[1-\alpha_{0}(\gamma)]^{T-1}.

The result does not depend on τ∗\tau^{*} because both α0​(γ)\alpha_{0}(\gamma) and β0​(γ)\beta_{0}(\gamma) are independent of the insertion time. ∎

The Type II error decomposes as a product: β0​(γ)\beta_{0}(\gamma) is the probability that the test fails to detect the target in the correct batch, and [1−α0​(γ)]T−1[1-\alpha_{0}(\gamma)]^{T-1} is the probability that none of the other batches trigger a false detection. Independence from τ∗\tau^{*} follows from the identical distribution of batch means.

Appendix F SGD Analysis

We consider the SGD setting where we observe model parameters θ0,θ1,…,θT\theta_{0},\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{T} with θt∈ℝd\theta_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. At each step tt, the update is θt=θt−1−ηt​gt\theta_{t}=\theta_{t-1}-\eta_{t}g_{t} where ηt>0\eta_{t}>0 is the learning rate and gtg_{t} is the batch gradient on dataset DtD_{t} of size ntn_{t}. The target z∗z^{*} lies in the data domain 𝒳\mathcal{X} and the insertion time τ\tau is known. We test:

𝐇𝟎\displaystyle\mathbf{H_{0}} :All samples in ​D1,…,DT​ are drawn i.i.d. from ​𝒟\displaystyle:\text{All samples in }D_{1},\ldots,D_{T}\text{ are drawn i.i.d.\ from }\mathcal{D}
𝐇𝟏τ\displaystyle\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}} :One sample in ​Dτ​ is replaced by ​z∗\displaystyle:\text{One sample in }D_{\tau}\text{ is replaced by }z^{*}

We assume that, conditioned on θt−1\theta_{t-1}, the batch gradient gtg_{t} is Gaussian with mean μg​(θt−1)\mu_{g}(\theta_{t-1}) and covariance Σg​(θt−1)/nt\Sigma_{g}(\theta_{t-1})/n_{t}. This approximation is justified by the central limit theorem when the batch aggregates gradients from many data points.

Notation. The loss function on data point xx with parameter θ\theta is denoted by ℓ⁡(θ,x)\ell(\theta;x). The batch gradient is gt=1nt​∑x∈Dt∇θℓ​(θt−1,x)g_{t}=\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{x\in D_{t}}\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{t-1};x). We denote by μg​(θ)\mu_{g}(\theta) and Σg​(θ)\Sigma_{g}(\theta) the mean and covariance of the batch gradient when scaled by nt\sqrt{n_{t}}, i.e., gt|θt−1∼𝒩⁡(μg​(θt−1),Σg​(θt−1)/nt)g_{t}\mid\theta_{t-1}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{g}(\theta_{t-1}),\Sigma_{g}(\theta_{t-1})/n_{t}).

F.1 Conditional Distributions

Lemma F.1 (Parameter Distribution Under 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}).

Under 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}, the conditional distribution of θt\theta_{t} given θt−1\theta_{t-1} is:

θt|θt−1,𝐇𝟎∼𝒩⁡(θt−1−ηt​μg​(θt−1),ηt2​Σg​(θt−1)nt).\theta_{t}\mid\theta_{t-1},\mathbf{H_{0}}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\theta_{t-1}-\eta_{t}\mu_{g}(\theta_{t-1}),\frac{\eta_{t}^{2}\Sigma_{g}(\theta_{t-1})}{n_{t}}\right).
Lemma F.2 (Parameter Distribution Under 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}}).

Under 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}}, the conditional distribution of θτ\theta_{\tau} given θτ−1\theta_{\tau-1} is:

θτ|θτ−1,𝐇𝟏τ∼𝒩⁡(θτ−1−ητ⋅(nτ−1)​μg​(θτ−1)+∇θℓ​(θτ−1,z∗)nτ,ητ2​(nτ−1)​Σg​(θτ−1)nτ2).\theta_{\tau}\mid\theta_{\tau-1},\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\theta_{\tau-1}-\eta_{\tau}\cdot\frac{(n_{\tau}-1)\mu_{g}(\theta_{\tau-1})+\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{\tau-1};z^{*})}{n_{\tau}},\frac{\eta_{\tau}^{2}(n_{\tau}-1)\Sigma_{g}(\theta_{\tau-1})}{n_{\tau}^{2}}\right).

For t≠τt\neq\tau, the conditional distribution is identical to that under 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}.

Proof.

Batch gradient under 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}}. Batch DτD_{\tau} contains (nτ−1)(n_{\tau}-1) samples from 𝒟\mathcal{D} and the fixed target z∗z^{*}. The batch gradient is:

gτ=1nτ​[∑i=1nτ−1∇θℓ​(θτ−1,xi)+∇θℓ​(θτ−1,z∗)].g_{\tau}=\frac{1}{n_{\tau}}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\tau}-1}\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{\tau-1};x_{i})+\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{\tau-1};z^{*})\right].

Under the Gaussian gradient assumption, the sum of (nτ−1)(n_{\tau}-1) i.i.d. Gaussian gradients has mean (nτ−1)​μg​(θτ−1)(n_{\tau}-1)\mu_{g}(\theta_{\tau-1}) and covariance (nτ−1)​Σg​(θτ−1)(n_{\tau}-1)\Sigma_{g}(\theta_{\tau-1}). Adding the fixed target gradient shifts the mean.

The result follows from θτ=θτ−1−ητ​gτ\theta_{\tau}=\theta_{\tau-1}-\eta_{\tau}g_{\tau}. ∎

F.2 Likelihood Ratio

Theorem F.3 (SGD Likelihood Ratio Simplification).

The likelihood ratio for testing 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}} against 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}} based on (θ0,…,θT)(\theta_{0},\ldots,\theta_{T}) satisfies:

p⁡(θ0,…,θT∣𝐇𝟏τ)p⁡(θ0,…,θT∣𝐇𝟎)=p⁡(θτ∣θτ−1,𝐇𝟏τ)p⁡(θτ∣θτ−1,𝐇𝟎).\frac{p(\theta_{0},\ldots,\theta_{T}\mid\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}})}{p(\theta_{0},\ldots,\theta_{T}\mid\mathbf{H_{0}})}=\frac{p(\theta_{\tau}\mid\theta_{\tau-1},\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}})}{p(\theta_{\tau}\mid\theta_{\tau-1},\mathbf{H_{0}})}.
Proof.

By the chain rule,

p⁡(θ0,…,θT∣H)p⁡(θ0)=∏t=1Tp⁡(θt∣θ0,…,θt−1,H).\frac{p(\theta_{0},\ldots,\theta_{T}\mid H)}{p(\theta_{0})}=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(\theta_{t}\mid\theta_{0},\ldots,\theta_{t-1},H).

The update θt=θt−1−ηt​gt\theta_{t}=\theta_{t-1}-\eta_{t}g_{t} implies that θt\theta_{t} depends on (θ0,…,θt−1)(\theta_{0},\ldots,\theta_{t-1}) only through θt−1\theta_{t-1}, since gtg_{t} depends on θt−1\theta_{t-1} and the samples in DtD_{t}. Thus

p⁡(θt∣θ0,…,θt−1,H)=p⁡(θt∣θt−1,H).p(\theta_{t}\mid\theta_{0},\ldots,\theta_{t-1},H)=p(\theta_{t}\mid\theta_{t-1},H).

The likelihood ratio becomes

LR=∏t=1Tp⁡(θt∣θt−1,𝐇𝟏τ)p⁡(θt∣θt−1,𝐇𝟎).\mathrm{LR}=\prod_{t=1}^{T}\frac{p(\theta_{t}\mid\theta_{t-1},\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}})}{p(\theta_{t}\mid\theta_{t-1},\mathbf{H_{0}})}.

For t<τt<\tau, the target has not been inserted, so both conditional distributions are identical and the ratio equals 1. For t>τt>\tau, batch DtD_{t} contains no target under either hypothesis, so conditioned on θt−1\theta_{t-1} the distributions coincide and the ratio equals 1. Only the term at t=τt=\tau contributes. ∎

Theorem F.4 (SGD Log Likelihood Ratio).

Define δg=∇θℓ​(θτ−1,z∗)−μg​(θτ−1)\delta_{g}=\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{\tau-1};z^{*})-\mu_{g}(\theta_{\tau-1}) and N=θτ−θτ−1+ητ​μg​(θτ−1)N=\theta_{\tau}-\theta_{\tau-1}+\eta_{\tau}\mu_{g}(\theta_{\tau-1}). The log likelihood ratio is:

log⁡LR\displaystyle\log\mathrm{LR} =−d2​log⁡(nτ−1nτ)−nτ2​(nτ−1)​ητ2​N⊤​Σg−1​N\displaystyle=-\frac{d}{2}\log\left(\frac{n_{\tau}-1}{n_{\tau}}\right)-\frac{n_{\tau}}{2(n_{\tau}-1)\eta_{\tau}^{2}}N^{\top}\Sigma_{g}^{-1}N
−nτ(nτ−1)​ητ​N⊤​Σg−1​δg−m∗2​(nτ−1)\displaystyle\quad-\frac{n_{\tau}}{(n_{\tau}-1)\eta_{\tau}}N^{\top}\Sigma_{g}^{-1}\delta_{g}-\frac{m^{*}}{2(n_{\tau}-1)}

where m∗=δg⊤​Σg−1​δgm^{*}=\delta_{g}^{\top}\Sigma_{g}^{-1}\delta_{g} is the Mahalanobis distance of the target gradient from the population mean. We denote this sequential test for SGD as SeMISGD\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{SGD}}.

Proof.

Conditional parameters. Let m0=θτ−1−ητ​μg​(θτ−1)m_{0}=\theta_{\tau-1}-\eta_{\tau}\mu_{g}(\theta_{\tau-1}) and m1=θτ−1−ητ​(nτ−1)​μg​(θτ−1)+∇θℓ​(θτ−1,z∗)nτm_{1}=\theta_{\tau-1}-\eta_{\tau}\frac{(n_{\tau}-1)\mu_{g}(\theta_{\tau-1})+\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{\tau-1};z^{*})}{n_{\tau}}. The covariances are V0=ητ2​ΣgnτV_{0}=\frac{\eta_{\tau}^{2}\Sigma_{g}}{n_{\tau}} and V1=ητ2​(nτ−1)​Σgnτ2V_{1}=\frac{\eta_{\tau}^{2}(n_{\tau}-1)\Sigma_{g}}{n_{\tau}^{2}}.

Mean difference.

m1−m0=−ητnτ​(∇θℓ​(θτ−1,z∗)−μg​(θτ−1))=−ητ​δgnτ.m_{1}-m_{0}=-\frac{\eta_{\tau}}{n_{\tau}}(\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{\tau-1};z^{*})-\mu_{g}(\theta_{\tau-1}))=-\frac{\eta_{\tau}\delta_{g}}{n_{\tau}}.

Log likelihood ratio. With N=θτ−m0N=\theta_{\tau}-m_{0}, expand the quadratic terms and substitute V0−1=nτητ2​Σg−1V_{0}^{-1}=\frac{n_{\tau}}{\eta_{\tau}^{2}}\Sigma_{g}^{-1}. Collecting terms yields the stated result. ∎

Theorem F.5 (Distribution of the Log Likelihood Ratio).

Under 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}:

N|θτ−1,𝐇𝟎∼𝒩⁡(0,ητ2​Σgnτ).N\mid\theta_{\tau-1},\mathbf{H_{0}}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\frac{\eta_{\tau}^{2}\Sigma_{g}}{n_{\tau}}\right).

Under 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}}:

N|θτ−1,𝐇𝟏τ∼𝒩⁡(−ητ​δgnτ,ητ2​(nτ−1)​Σgnτ2).N\mid\theta_{\tau-1},\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(-\frac{\eta_{\tau}\delta_{g}}{n_{\tau}},\frac{\eta_{\tau}^{2}(n_{\tau}-1)\Sigma_{g}}{n_{\tau}^{2}}\right).
Proof.

Under 𝐇𝟎\mathbf{H_{0}}, θτ|θτ−1∼𝒩⁡(m0,V0)\theta_{\tau}\mid\theta_{\tau-1}\sim\mathcal{N}(m_{0},V_{0}) with m0=θτ−1−ητ​μg​(θτ−1)m_{0}=\theta_{\tau-1}-\eta_{\tau}\mu_{g}(\theta_{\tau-1}). Since N=θτ−m0N=\theta_{\tau}-m_{0}, we have N∼𝒩⁡(0,V0)N\sim\mathcal{N}(0,V_{0}).

Under 𝐇𝟏τ\mathbf{H_{1}^{\tau}}, θτ|θτ−1∼𝒩⁡(m1,V1)\theta_{\tau}\mid\theta_{\tau-1}\sim\mathcal{N}(m_{1},V_{1}). Thus N=θτ−m0∼𝒩⁡(m1−m0,V1)N=\theta_{\tau}-m_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(m_{1}-m_{0},V_{1}). Recalling that m1−m0=−ητ​δgnτm_{1}-m_{0}=-\frac{\eta_{\tau}\delta_{g}}{n_{\tau}}, we have the stated mean and covariance. ∎

F.3 Application to Linear Regression

For linear regression with squared loss ℓ⁡(θ,(x,y))=12​(y−θ⊤​x)2\ell(\theta;(x,y))=\frac{1}{2}(y-\theta^{\top}x)^{2} and Gaussian covariates x∼𝒩⁡(0,Σx)x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{x}):

Lemma F.6 (Mean Gradient).

Let Δ=θ−θ∗\Delta=\theta-\theta^{*}. The mean gradient is μg​(θ)=Σx​Δ\mu_{g}(\theta)=\Sigma_{x}\Delta.

Proof.

Let ∇θℓ​(θ,(x,y))=(θ⊤​x−y)​x=(θ⊤​x−θ∗⁣⊤​x−ε)​x=(Δ⊤​x−ε)​x\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta;(x,y))=(\theta^{\top}x-y)x=(\theta^{\top}x-\theta^{*\top}x-\varepsilon)x=(\Delta^{\top}x-\varepsilon)x. Taking expectations:

μg​(θ)=𝔼⁡[(Δ⊤​x)​x]−𝔼⁡[ε]​𝔼​[x]=𝔼⁡[x​x⊤]​Δ=Σx​Δ.\mu_{g}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}[(\Delta^{\top}x)x]-\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon]\mathbb{E}[x]=\mathbb{E}[xx^{\top}]\Delta=\Sigma_{x}\Delta.

∎

Lemma F.7 (Gradient Covariance).

The covariance of the per-sample gradient is:

Σg​(θ)=(σε2+Δ⊤​Σx​Δ)​Σx+Σx​Δ​Δ⊤​Σx.\Sigma_{g}(\theta)=(\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}+\Delta^{\top}\Sigma_{x}\Delta)\Sigma_{x}+\Sigma_{x}\Delta\Delta^{\top}\Sigma_{x}.
Proof.

The second moment is 𝔼⁡[g​g⊤]=𝔼⁡[(Δ⊤​x−ε)2​x​x⊤]\mathbb{E}[gg^{\top}]=\mathbb{E}[(\Delta^{\top}x-\varepsilon)^{2}xx^{\top}]. Since ε⟂x\varepsilon\perp x and 𝔼⁡[ε]=0\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon]=0:

𝔼⁡[g​g⊤]=𝔼⁡[(Δ⊤​x)2​x​x⊤]+σε2​Σx.\mathbb{E}[gg^{\top}]=\mathbb{E}[(\Delta^{\top}x)^{2}xx^{\top}]+\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}\Sigma_{x}.

Using Isserlis’ theorem for the fourth moment of Gaussian xx:

𝔼⁡[(Δ⊤​x)2​x​x⊤]=(Δ⊤​Σx​Δ)​Σx+2​Σx​Δ​Δ⊤​Σx.\mathbb{E}[(\Delta^{\top}x)^{2}xx^{\top}]=(\Delta^{\top}\Sigma_{x}\Delta)\Sigma_{x}+2\Sigma_{x}\Delta\Delta^{\top}\Sigma_{x}.

The covariance is Σg=𝔼⁡[g​g⊤]−μg​μg⊤\Sigma_{g}=\mathbb{E}[gg^{\top}]-\mu_{g}\mu_{g}^{\top}. Subtracting μg​μg⊤=Σx​Δ​Δ⊤​Σx\mu_{g}\mu_{g}^{\top}=\Sigma_{x}\Delta\Delta^{\top}\Sigma_{x} yields the result. ∎

Corollary F.8 (Gradient Statistics at Optimum).

At θ=θ∗\theta=\theta^{*}, we have Δ=0\Delta=0, so μg​(θ∗)=0\mu_{g}(\theta^{*})=0 and Σg​(θ∗)=σε2​Σx\Sigma_{g}(\theta^{*})=\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}\Sigma_{x}.

Lemma F.9 (Target Gradient Deviation).

At θ=θ∗\theta=\theta^{*}, the target gradient is ∇θℓ​(θ∗,(x∗,y∗))=−ε∗​x∗\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta^{*};(x^{*},y^{*}))=-\varepsilon^{*}x^{*} where ε∗\varepsilon^{*} is the target residual. The deviation from the population mean is δg=−ε∗​x∗\delta_{g}=-\varepsilon^{*}x^{*}.

Proof.

At optimum, ∇θℓ=(θ∗⁣⊤​x∗−y∗)​x∗=−ε∗​x∗\nabla_{\theta}\ell=(\theta^{*\top}x^{*}-y^{*})x^{*}=-\varepsilon^{*}x^{*}. Since μg​(θ∗)=0\mu_{g}(\theta^{*})=0, δg=−ε∗​x∗\delta_{g}=-\varepsilon^{*}x^{*}. ∎

Theorem F.10 (Detectability at Optimum).

At θ=θ∗\theta=\theta^{*}, the Mahalanobis distance of the target gradient is:

m∗=(ε∗)2σε2⋅(x∗)⊤​Σx−1​x∗.m^{*}=\frac{(\varepsilon^{*})^{2}}{\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}}\cdot(x^{*})^{\top}\Sigma_{x}^{-1}x^{*}.

This factors as product of a label outlier score (ε∗/σε)2(\varepsilon^{*}/\sigma_{\varepsilon})^{2} and a feature leverage score (x∗)⊤​Σx−1​x∗.(x^{*})^{\top}\Sigma_{x}^{-1}x^{*}.

Proof.

Substituting into m∗=δg⊤​Σg​(θ∗)−1​δgm^{*}=\delta_{g}^{\top}\Sigma_{g}(\theta^{*})^{-1}\delta_{g}:

m∗=(−ε∗​x∗)⊤​(σε2​Σx)−1​(−ε∗​x∗)=(ε∗)2σε2​(x∗)⊤​Σx−1​x∗.m^{*}=(-\varepsilon^{*}x^{*})^{\top}(\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}\Sigma_{x})^{-1}(-\varepsilon^{*}x^{*})=\frac{(\varepsilon^{*})^{2}}{\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}}(x^{*})^{\top}\Sigma_{x}^{-1}x^{*}.

∎

Samples with large residuals (relative to population noise) and unusual feature vectors (relative to population covariance) are most detectable.

Appendix H Additional Experiments

This appendix provides additional experimental results supporting the main paper. We examine the GLR test for unknown insertion time, validation on SGD, sensitivity to unknown parameters, and the multivariate setting.

H.1 Unknown Insertion Time

This section provides additional results for the sequential tests when the insertion time τ\tau is unknown. We use n=10n=10, μ=0\mu=0, σ=1\sigma=1, and target z∗z^{*} with Mahalanobis distance 3. Power comparisons as a function of TT and signal strength appear in the main text (Figure 2).

Figure 4 shows ROC curves for different values of TT. As TT increases, the gap between SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*} and the other methods widens, while SeMIUnif\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{Unif}} and SeMImax\mathrm{SeMI}^{\max} maintain an advantage over Final Observation.

Uniformly Sampled τ\tau.

The preceding experiments fix the insertion time τ\tau and evaluate the GLR test that maximizes over candidate values. We now consider the composite hypothesis setting where the insertion time is itself random: under 𝐇𝟏\mathbf{H_{1}}, the target z∗z^{*} is inserted at τ∼Uniform⁡(1,T)\tau\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(1,T). This formulation captures scenarios where the auditor has no prior knowledge about when a datapoint might have been added.

Figure 5 shows ROC curves and power as a function of signal strength. The qualitative behavior matches the fixed-τ\tau case: SeMImax\mathrm{SeMI}^{\max} outperforms the Final Observation baseline at large Mahalanobis distances, while SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*} (which knows the true τ\tau) provides an upper bound.

Figure 6 displays power versus TT. The gap between SeMI∗\mathrm{SeMI}^{*} and SeMImax\mathrm{SeMI}^{\max} persists, confirming that estimating the insertion time introduces a cost even when τ\tau is uniformly distributed.

H.2 SGD Validation

We validate the extension to SGD (Section 4) using linear regression with d=5d=5 features, T=10T=10 updates, batch size n=50n=50, and learning rate η=0.05\eta=0.05.

Figure 7(a) shows ROC curves for insertion at τ=5\tau=5. SeMISGD\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{SGD}} outperforms the Delta and Back-Front heuristics from Jagielski et al. (2023).

Figure 7(b) shows power as a function of insertion time τ\tau. The Back-Front statistic maintains constant power with respect to τ\tau because it depends only on endpoints and gradient effects persist in convex landscapes. The Delta statistic shows decreasing power as τ\tau increases: early in training, gradient magnitudes are larger, producing stronger signals. SeMISGD\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{SGD}} maintains high power across all τ\tau.

H.3 Multivariate Setting

We test the extension to dd-dimensional Gaussian data (Appendix B). Parameters: n=10n=10, T=5T=5, τ=3\tau=3, target z∗z^{*} with Mahalanobis distance 3 from the mean.

Figure 8(a) displays the decision boundary in d=2d=2. Figure 8(b) shows that power remains constant as dimension dd increases from 2 to 50. For a fixed Mahalanobis distance, the test statistic depends on the projection onto the target direction, making power independent of ambient dimension.

H.4 DP-SGD Fine-tuning: ROC Curves

This section provides ROC curves for the privacy auditing experiments on DP-SGD fine-tuning (Section 5). We show results for Fashion-MNIST at two privacy levels: non-private (ε=∞\varepsilon=\infty) and private (ε=1.0\varepsilon=1.0).

Figure 9(a) shows the non-private setting. SeMISGD\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{SGD}} and SeMImax\mathrm{SeMI}^{\max} both achieve near-perfect discrimination (AUC ≈1.0\approx 1.0), while the heuristic baselines perform substantially worse (Back-Front AUC ≈0.80\approx 0.80, Delta AUC ≈0.65\approx 0.65). This confirms that the likelihood ratio test exploits gradient information more effectively than loss-based heuristics.

Figure 9(b) shows the private setting (ε=1.0\varepsilon=1.0). All methods degrade due to the DP noise, but SeMISGD\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{SGD}} maintains an advantage (AUC =0.60=0.60) over baselines (AUC ≈0.51\approx 0.51–0.530.53). The gap is most pronounced at low false positive rates, which are relevant for privacy auditing where conservative bounds are desired.

H.5 Effect of Insertion Time Selection

The main text reports privacy lower bounds averaged over insertion times τ∈{1,…,T}\tau\in\{1,\ldots,T\}. Here we compare this averaging strategy against selecting the best τ\tau post hoc, i.e., reporting the tightest bound across all insertion times.

Figure 10 shows results for Fashion-MNIST. Solid lines show the averaged estimates; dashed lines show the maximum (best τ\tau) estimates. For SeMISGD\mathrm{SeMI}^{\mathrm{SGD}}, selecting the best τ\tau yields substantially tighter bounds, particularly at moderate privacy levels (ε∈[0.5,2]\varepsilon\in[0.5,2]). The gap between Average and Max indicates that some insertion times are more favorable for auditing than others.

This observation suggests that an auditor who can choose when to insert the target, or who audits at multiple insertion times and reports the best result, can obtain tighter privacy lower bounds. Determining which τ\tau is optimal a priori for a given architecture and dataset remains an open question for future work.
